chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## The Discipline Test

When Bitcoin's fourth halving arrived on 19 April 2024, cutting the per-block mining reward from 6.25 BTC to 3.125 BTC overnight, the event functioned less as a surprise than as a stress test — a moment that separated operators who had prepared from those who had not. CleanSpark, Inc. (NASDAQ: CLSK), headquartered in Las Vegas, Nevada, had spent the preceding eighteen months constructing precisely the kind of operating posture that a halving rewards: multi-exahash scale, a fleet refresh toward Bitmain's energy-efficient S21 generation, and long-term power purchase agreements anchoring electricity cost below the threshold at which compressed unit economics become existential.

That posture, and the strategic questions it raises for the years ahead, forms the subject of this dossier.

## Company at a Glance

CleanSpark's origins lie far from the industrial data-center campuses it now operates across Georgia, Mississippi, New York, Tennessee, Wyoming, and other US states. The corporate entity traces its lineage to a predecessor incorporated around 1987 as Stratean; it reached its current form through a reverse merger and a multi-year corporate evolution that passed through an energy-software business before arriving, under the leadership of Zach Bradford, at pure-play Bitcoin mining.

Bradford joined the company in a CFO capacity and assumed the chief executive role in 2017. Over the following years he executed one of the more consequential strategic pivots in the small-cap digital-asset universe: unwinding the energy-software predecessor, deploying capital into ASIC mining hardware and owned-and-leased data center infrastructure, and building a vertically integrated energy procurement function capable of sourcing electricity at competitive all-in costs through direct grid-connection arrangements and long-term PPA contracts with US utilities and independent power producers.

The operating model that emerged is structurally simple and operationally demanding. CleanSpark deploys industrial-scale Bitcoin mining ASICs — principally Bitmain Antminer S19, S21, S21 Pro, and S21 XP generations, supplemented by Whatsminer hardware — at its owned and leased campuses. The company earns revenue by mining Bitcoin at the protocol-level network reward, then selling produced coin to spot markets through institutional trading desks including Coinbase Prime. There are no traditional customers; the counterparty is the Bitcoin network itself, and the principal performance variables are hash rate scale (measured in exahashes per second), energy efficiency (joules per terahash), all-in electricity cost (dollars per megawatt-hour), fleet uptime and utilization, network difficulty growth, and Bitcoin price.

## The Halving and the Hash Rate Scaling Race

The April 2024 halving compressed unit economics across the industry in the sharpest possible terms. Where an operator running 30 J/TH hardware at $40/MWh had previously mined at a workable margin on 6.25 BTC per block, the halved reward demanded either a lower electricity cost, a more efficient fleet, greater scale, or some combination of all three. Marginal operators — those running older S19-series hardware at elevated power costs — faced immediate pressure to curtail or exit. The episode accelerated consolidation toward the handful of operators capable of absorbing the reward compression and continuing to expand hash rate.

CleanSpark pursued hash rate scaling through 2024 and into 2025, refreshing its ASIC fleet toward the S21 and S21 XP generations, which deliver materially lower joules-per-terahash ratings than the prior cohort. The fleet refresh simultaneously reduced operating cost per bitcoin mined and improved the company's competitive position on the industry efficiency curve — a critical variable as network difficulty continued its secular upward drift through post-halving periods of miner consolidation.

## The AI/HPC Optionality Thesis

Alongside the halving-era operating discipline, CleanSpark entered the frame of a thesis that has reconfigured the Bitcoin mining industry's self-narrative: the AI and high-performance computing pivot. Across the peer set — Core Scientific (CORZ), Iris Energy (IREN), TeraWulf (WULF), Bitfarms (BITF), Hut 8 (HUT), Marathon Digital (MARA), Riot Platforms (RIOT), and Bitdeer (BTDR) — the logic was consistent: power-secured campus footprints built for Bitcoin mining share fundamental infrastructure characteristics with the colocation and hyperscale data centers in acute demand for AI training and inference workloads. Secured power interconnects, built-out transmission infrastructure, and cooling capacity are the gating constraints for AI data-center development; Bitcoin miners, having assembled them at scale, found themselves in possession of optionality that the market had not fully priced when the campus build-outs were initially funded.

CleanSpark's positioning on this thesis — the timing, scope, and customer engagement disclosures behind any AI/HPC conversion of campus capacity — remains a principal open question through the dossier's research horizon.

## What This Dossier Asks

Six questions frame the analytical work that follows. First, how did post-halving unit economics evolve in practice — what were the realized electricity costs, fleet efficiency metrics, and cost-per-bitcoin-mined figures that Bradford's operating discipline produced? Second, how did hash rate scaling execution track against management's stated targets, and where does the company sit on the industry efficiency curve against its peer set? Third, what is the state of the AI/HPC pivot optionality — has CleanSpark disclosed customer engagements, conversion timelines, or capital allocation toward AI/HPC hosting, and how does its posture compare to peers who moved earlier? Fourth, is the capital structure adequate through Bitcoin price cycles, given the company's reliance on ATM equity issuance alongside operating cash flow? Fifth, what does CleanSpark's competitive position look like against RIOT, MARA, CORZ, IREN, WULF, BITF, HUT, and BTDR across the dimensions that matter post-halving: scale, efficiency, energy cost, and strategic clarity? And sixth, what is the Bradford strategic narrative — the through-line from energy-software predecessor to multi-exahash Bitcoin miner to potential AI-infrastructure operator — and does it hold together as a durable value-creation thesis or a sequence of opportunistic pivots?

Those questions, and the evidence assembled to answer them, constitute the chapters that follow.

chapters.title: From energy-software predecessor through Bitcoin mining pivot to multi-EH/s scaling
chapters.body:
## A Shell's Long Wandering: From SmartData to Stratean, 1987–2016

The corporate entity that would eventually become one of North America's largest Bitcoin mining operators began life in Nevada in October 1987 as SmartData Corporation, incorporated to distribute computer hardware and software to small businesses and to offer ancillary staff-leasing and benefits services. The venture never found its footing. When its founding chief executive, Paul Gambles, died in 1992, operations were suspended and the company drifted into dormancy, its Nevada charter intact but commercially inert for more than two decades.

The shell stirred back to life in March 2014, when a small team led by Matthew Schultz reactivated it in the alternative-energy sector. Schultz, who had studied at Weber State University and would remain a defining figure in the company's arc, rechristened the entity Stratean Inc. and focused it on a patented stratified downdraft gasifier technology designed to convert biomass and waste feedstocks into usable energy. The ticker changed to SRTN on the OTC market, and the company began assembling a renewable-energy portfolio — niche, capital-light, and small.

The decisive transformation came in July 2016. Stratean executed a $36-million all-equity asset purchase agreement to acquire CleanSpark Holdings LLC, CleanSpark LLC, CleanSpark Technologies LLC, and Specialized Energy Solutions — a cluster of companies built around proprietary microgrid software called **mPulse**. The price was structured as six million shares plus 4.5 million warrants at a $1.50 strike. By November 14, 2016, Stratean had renamed itself **CleanSpark, Inc.** and changed its OTC ticker to CLSK, signalling that the microgrid software identity, not the gasifier heritage, would define the new chapter.

Arriving simultaneously with the merger was **Zachary Bradford**, who entered a consulting agreement on July 1, 2016 as President and Chief Financial Officer. Bradford held a B.S. and M.S. in accounting from Southern Utah University and had previously served as CFO at Be At TV, Inc. and Epic Stores Corp. before founding a Nevada accounting practice in 2013. He brought public-company reporting discipline to an organisation that had previously operated closer to a development-stage venture.

## The Microgrid Years: mPulse, mVSO, and the Limits of Energy Software, 2016–2020

The mPulse platform that CleanSpark brought into the merger was a monitoring and control system for distributed energy resources — solar arrays, battery storage, and demand-response loads — knitted together by a forecasting and real-time optimisation engine. The company had earned early validation through a deployment at the Marine Corps' **Camp Pendleton School of Infantry** in 2013 and claimed more than $14 million in cumulative revenue and $8 million invested in platform development by the time of the Stratean deal. In May 2019, it released a production version of the **mVSO (Microgrid Value Stream Optimizer)**, a SaaS-oriented analytics layer for engineering, procurement and construction firms designing commercial and industrial microgrids, and followed that October with a subscription offering for the same EPC market.

The business was real but slow. Field deployments trickled in — a California City off-grid solar-and-storage installation in June 2020, a 222-kW photovoltaic system paired with a Tesla 111-kW/223-kWh Powerpack in Costa Rica in September 2020 — but the commercial scale required to justify a public-company overhead structure proved elusive. In October 2019, Schultz stepped back from the CEO role he had held since the company's March 2014 reactivation, assuming the title of Executive Chairman. Bradford was elevated to Chief Executive Officer. The transition was publicly framed as a move to accelerate "profitability and commercialisation of its microgrid technology," but the strategic reset that actually followed ran in a different direction entirely.

## The Pivot: College Park, December 2020

On December 10, 2020, CleanSpark announced the acquisition of **ATL Data Centers**, a Bitcoin mining operation situated near Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in College Park, Georgia, for up to $19.4 million in common stock. The facility housed 3,471 ASIC mining units running at approximately 190 petahashes per second across 23 mobile data centres, drawing 9.6 megawatts of contracted capacity with expansion headroom to 50 MW. In the eight days between closing and Bradford's first operational update on December 18, the machines produced roughly 10 bitcoin — worth approximately $200,000 at prevailing prices.

The initial framing positioned Bitcoin mining as a proving ground for mPulse's energy-management capabilities, the suggestion being that CleanSpark's software edge would translate into lower power costs and better uptime than mining-only competitors. That narrative was quietly shelved over the following eighteen months as it became clear that hash-rate scale and electricity procurement, not microgrid software differentiation, determined competitive position in Bitcoin mining. The energy-software division continued on paper through June 30, 2022, when CleanSpark formally exited it; from that point forward the company described itself as having "operated in the bitcoin mining sector since December 2020."

## Compounding Hash Rate: 2021–2023

From the 190 PH/s base at ATL, CleanSpark scaled aggressively through a combination of ASIC purchase agreements and strategic acquisitions of established infrastructure.

| Period | Operating Hash Rate | Key Event |
|---|---|---|
| December 2020 | ~0.19 EH/s | ATL Data Centers acquisition closes |
| December 2021 | ~2.1 EH/s | 20,900 machines; ~10 BTC/day production rate |
| September 2022 | ~3.7 EH/s | 37,000+ machines; 140 MW capacity |
| October 2022 | ~4.7 EH/s | Mawson/Sandersville acquisition closes |
| July 2023 | ~8.0 EH/s | — |
| FY2023 full year | ~10 EH/s | 6,903 BTC mined for the fiscal year |
| February 2024 | 10 EH/s operational | S21 deployment ramp underway |

The single most consequential acquisition during this phase was the **Mawson Infrastructure Group Sandersville, Georgia campus**, announced September 9, 2022 and closed October 11, 2022 for up to $42.5 million — structured as $26.5 million cash, $11 million in CleanSpark common stock, and $5 million in seller financing. Mawson had built the site from the ground up before deciding to concentrate its capital in Pennsylvania and Texas; CleanSpark acquired 80 MW of operating infrastructure with expansion potential to 230 MW and 6,468 ASICs.

> "The site is nothing but impressive," Bradford said at the time of closing.

Georgia cemented itself as the principal operating footprint — the state's regulated utility environment, available industrial land, and CleanSpark's accumulating relationships with local electric municipal cooperatives gave the company a procurement and permitting advantage it would exploit for years.

## The S21 Wager and the April 2024 Halving

By October 2023, with the fourth Bitcoin halving roughly six months away, management made a forward commitment that defined the subsequent scaling story: a purchase of approximately 4.4 EH/s worth of Bitmain **Antminer S21** machines, a generation running at roughly 17.5 joules per terahash — nearly 20 percent more efficient than the S19 XP units that had themselves displaced the original S19 fleet. The S21 order set a path toward 20 EH/s that Bradford had guided publicly for the first half of 2024.

> "Efficiency is the most important variable as we head into the halving," Bradford told investors ahead of the April event.

The halving arrived on schedule, cutting the per-block reward from 6.25 BTC to 3.125 BTC and compressing unit economics across every publicly traded miner. CleanSpark's preparation showed in the balance sheet: the company entered the event with nearly $700 million in combined cash and bitcoin holdings and, by management's account, virtually no debt. The older S19j Pro fleet was liquidated to the secondary market post-halving; S21 Pro units filled the vacated rack space.

Operational execution in the twelve months surrounding the halving was captured in a single data point: CleanSpark mined approximately 7,100 BTC in fiscal year 2024 — more than the ~6,900 BTC produced in fiscal year 2023, even as the protocol-level reward per block had been cut in half. Hash rate scale had absorbed the reward compression. On June 18, 2024, the company closed an acquisition of **five additional turnkey facilities in rural Georgia** — 60 combined megawatts, each sized between 8 MW and 15 MW and served by interruptible-load power purchase agreements with local electric cooperatives — for $25.8 million cash. The deal pushed the Georgia footprint past 400 MW and locked in the 20 EH/s milestone.

> "These sites lock in the achievement of our mid-year target of achieving 20 EH/s of operating hashrate," Bradford said at announcement.

By December 2024 the operating fleet stood at 37.5 EH/s. Full-year fiscal 2024 revenue reached $379 million, a 125 percent increase year-over-year, as hash-rate growth and a recovering Bitcoin price ran in tandem.

## Power Footprint and the AI/HPC Horizon

The hash rate trajectory continued into 2025 as CleanSpark extended its geographic footprint beyond Georgia into Mississippi, Tennessee, Wyoming, and upstate New York. The multi-site, multi-state expansion gave the company more than 750 MW of contracted or operational capacity and, crucially, a portfolio of power-secured campuses that management began describing in terms extending beyond Bitcoin mining alone.

The power-secured campus footprint — already built, already grid-connected, already permitted — positioned CleanSpark to participate in the broader industry conversation about repurposing or co-locating high-density compute infrastructure for artificial-intelligence and high-performance-computing workloads. Peers including Core Scientific, Iris Energy, and TeraWulf had moved variously toward binding AI/HPC hosting agreements; CleanSpark's management characterised its own positioning as optionality to be exercised selectively, contingent on customer economics and capital-return discipline. Whether that optionality would translate into contracted revenue before or after the snapshot date of this dossier remained the defining open question in the company's strategic narrative — one that Bradford, after eight years steering the company from microgrid-software shell to multi-exahash Bitcoin miner, had left to his successor to answer.

chapters.title: ASIC fleet, hash rate, energy procurement, data center facilities
chapters.body:
## The ASIC Refresh Imperative

By the time the fourth Bitcoin halving arrived in April 2024 — cutting the block reward from 6.25 BTC to 3.125 BTC overnight — CleanSpark had spent the prior eighteen months repositioning its entire hardware estate around a single conviction: that post-halving survival would be decided on the efficiency of the machines in the ground, not the size of the balance sheet above it. The company's fleet in fiscal 2023 averaged 26.4 joules per terahash. Chief Executive Zach Bradford, speaking at the FY2023 earnings call, acknowledged the gap plainly and pointed toward the path forward.

> "Our fleet-wide efficiency is now 26.4 joules per terahash, and we expect to continue to see sustained improvements in our efficiency with Sandersville coming online in the next few months."

The engineering response to that gap unfolded across a series of Bitmain purchase agreements that became the structural backbone of the company's capital programme. In October 2023 CleanSpark acquired approximately 4.4 exahashes per second of Antminer S21 miners — rated at 17.5 J/TH, a meaningful step down from the S19-generation machines it was retiring — with delivery staged to coincide with the Sandersville site expansion in Georgia. Three months later, in January 2024, the company entered a strategic framework agreement for up to 160,000 S21 units at $16 per terahash, with an initial batch of 60,000 units committed. The decisive upgrade came in April 2024, one week before the halving itself, when CleanSpark amended that agreement to substitute 100,000 of those units with Antminer S21 Pro miners — a machine rated at 15.0 J/TH, a 14 percent improvement over the base S21 — at the same $16/TH price already locked. The amendment added roughly 3.4 EH/s of incremental capacity, bringing committed S21-class hash rate to approximately 23.4 EH/s. Delivery ran from June through December 2024.

The S21 XP Immersion — sub-15 J/TH and designed for liquid-cooled deployment — arrived as the fleet's efficiency apex, reserved for the company's purpose-built immersion sites at Cheyenne, Wyoming and the first phase of its Jackson, Tennessee campus.

## Hash Rate: From Challenger to Scale

The numerical trajectory of CleanSpark's hash rate scaling across the twenty-four months following the FY2023 close is, by any industrial measure, exceptional. From 12.5 EH/s at December 2023, the company crossed 17 EH/s by the end of the March 2024 quarter, crossed 22 EH/s by the end of June 2024, and exited fiscal year 2024 — the September 30 close — at 33.5 EH/s, representing 287.9 percent growth year-over-year. The pace did not slow. December 2024 month-end reached 39.1 EH/s; January 2025 crossed 40 EH/s for the first time; May 2025 stood at 45.6 EH/s on a growing base of 230,232 deployed machines. The 50 EH/s milestone — a threshold Bradford had identified publicly as a long-term target in the Q1 FY2024 call — was achieved in June 2025, making CleanSpark the first U.S.-listed public miner to self-operate that scale without co-location or third-party hosting arrangements.

| Month-End | Operating Hash Rate (EH/s) | Deployed Units | Avg Fleet Efficiency (J/TH) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dec 2023 | 12.5 | — | ~26.4 |
| Mar 2024 | 17.0+ | — | — |
| Jun 2024 | 22.0+ | — | — |
| Sep 2024 | 33.5 | — | — |
| Dec 2024 | 39.1 | 201,808 | 18.06 |
| Jan 2025 | 40.1 | 217,272 | 17.37 |
| Feb 2025 | 40.7 | 198,715 | 17.07 |
| Mar 2025 | 42.4 | 205,412 | 17.03 |
| May 2025 | 45.6 | 230,232 | 16.71 |
| Jun 2025 | 50.0 | — | — |

Fleet efficiency improved by 33.3 percent between December 2023 and December 2024, as legacy S19j, S19j Pro, and S19j Pro+ machines were progressively retired to the secondary market and replaced by S21 Pro units. The average efficiency at May 2025 — 16.71 J/TH — reflected a fleet that was predominantly S21 Pro with growing S21 XP Immersion deployment at the company's liquid-cooled sites.

## The Georgia Engine Room

Georgia remained the operational centre of gravity throughout this period, contributing the majority of hash rate and providing the template for CleanSpark's interruptible-load energy procurement model. The company operated six distinct Georgia campuses by mid-2024: the original College Park facility at 47 megawatts; the Norcross campus, an 87,000-square-foot former Sprint/Nextel data centre repurposed for immersion-cooled mining at 20 MW; Washington at 36 MW; the Dalton campus serving approximately 2.4 EH/s of capacity through three sites on Dalton Utilities' city-owned network; and Sandersville, the flagship at 150 MW and the largest single facility in the portfolio. In June 2024, CleanSpark acquired five additional rural Georgia sites from LN Energy for $25.8 million, adding approximately 60 megawatts of combined capacity under interruptible-load power purchase agreements.

Sandersville merits particular attention. Acquired from Mawson Infrastructure in 2022, the facility reached its 100-megawatt Phase 1 energisation in February 2024 — the catalyst Bradford had referenced in his efficiency guidance months earlier — and expanded to its full 150 MW nameplate by late 2024. Utility service is provided by the Municipal Electric Authority of Georgia, which supplies the facility through Washington EMC and Sandersville Electric as distribution co-operatives, with Oglethorpe Power providing bulk generation backstop. The Dalton campuses operate under Dalton Utilities, the city-owned municipal provider, at rates that reflect the municipality's direct generation and transmission ownership.

The Georgia state total reached and sustained more than 400 MW of operated capacity by the end of calendar 2024, underpinned by what Bradford described as the grid-service structure that makes interruptible load commercially attractive to both operator and utility:

> "We also provide an important grid service because our load is interruptible and can be returned to the community at a moment's notice."

## Expanding the Campus Footprint

Mississippi entered the portfolio in February 2024 when CleanSpark acquired three facilities from Makerstar Capital for $19.8 million: sites at Vicksburg (17,500 square feet, 5 acres), Wiggins (10,500 square feet, 9 acres), and Meridian (5,500 square feet, 5 acres), together representing approximately 44 MW. A further two Clinton, Mississippi sites totalling 16.5 MW followed in September 2024 for $5.775 million, both carrying S21 Pro deployments and projected combined output of approximately 1 EH/s. Mississippi's total portfolio stood at roughly 60.5 MW across five facilities.

Wyoming offered a different acquisition logic. In August and September 2024, CleanSpark acquired two Cheyenne-area sites — 30 MW and 45 MW respectively — from MineOne Wyoming LLC, a Chinese-owned operator that the Biden administration had ordered to divest following national-security concerns about the facilities' proximity to Francis E. Warren Air Force Base. The total acquisition price was $18.75 million. Both Wyoming sites were purpose-built for S21 XP Immersion deployment, with the combined 75 MW expected to contribute approximately 5 EH/s at completion; contracted power was subsequently expanded to 110 MW by February 2025.

Tennessee arrived through a larger structural transaction: the acquisition of GRIID Infrastructure, closed October 30, 2024, at an enterprise value of $155 million. GRIID's portfolio sat entirely within Tennessee Valley Authority service territory — a deliberate fit with CleanSpark's preference for utility relationships offering predictable and affordable long-term power. The acquired sites included facilities at Limestone, Maynardville, and Lenoir City, with post-closing expansion plans targeting 100 MW by year-end 2024, 200 MW through 2025, and 400 MW by 2026. CleanSpark subsequently acquired seven additional Tennessee locations for $30 million, including the Jackson facility — a 60-megawatt site where Phase 1 deployed 12 MW of S21 XP Immersion capacity yielding approximately 0.7 EH/s, with Phase 2 targeting a further 48 MW of air-cooled S21 Pro additions. New York, by contrast, was a chapter that closed: the Massena co-location within the Coinmint hydroelectric facility was fully divested before February 28, 2025, completing the transition to a portfolio described as 100 percent owned and self-operated.

By February 2025, total contracted megawatts stood at 915 MW across this multi-state footprint, rising to 987 MW at the May 2025 operational update.

## Energy Procurement Architecture and Power Cost Discipline

The financial consequence of this geographic diversity — and of the interruptible-load structuring in Georgia — showed clearly in CleanSpark's electricity cost reports. The company carried an all-in blended rate of $0.048 per kilowatt-hour in both fiscal year 2023 and fiscal year 2024, with the Georgia wholly-owned sites achieving wholesale rates as low as $0.013 per kilowatt-hour in favourable dispatch periods during the March 2024 quarter. The all-in blended rate for Q2 FY2024 was $0.043 per kilowatt-hour; Q3 FY2024 averaged $0.048 per kilowatt-hour. Management guided a $0.030–$0.040 per kilowatt-hour range as the forward target entering the post-halving period.

The cost discipline translated into a marginal cost to mine Bitcoin of approximately $34,000 per coin at owned facilities through Q1 and Q2 of fiscal 2025, rising to approximately $44,806 per coin by Q3 FY2025 as network difficulty growth compressed the network-level margin. Through fiscal year 2025 the company produced 7,024 BTC across the calendar year against a growing hash rate base, generating revenue of $766.3 million — a 102 percent year-over-year increase. By May 2025, Bradford summarised the positioning in terms that made the competitive logic explicit:

> "As other players shift direction or decelerate growth, CleanSpark has doubled down on being the only remaining pure-play, vertically integrated Bitcoin miner in the public markets."

The claim — that vertical integration of power procurement, ASIC ownership, and data centre operation could sustain industry-leading unit economics through both halving compression and network difficulty escalation — was, at the frozen snapshot, the central test the operational infrastructure had been built to answer.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, post-halving unit economics, capital structure, ATM dilution
chapters.body:
## The Revenue Engine: Hash Rate Times Bitcoin Price

CleanSpark's financial architecture reduced to a structural equation that management repeated across every earnings call: hash rate deployed, multiplied by the Bitcoin spot price at block reward receipt, minus electricity consumed per terahash. Everything else—depreciation schedules, SG&A leverage, equipment financing costs, ATM facility mechanics—was secondary noise around that signal. The company's revenue line, from fiscal 2021 through the post-halving normalisation, tracked that equation with near-perfect fidelity.

For the fiscal year ended September 30, 2022, CleanSpark reported mining revenue of approximately $116 million, a figure that masked a violent intra-period compression: Bitcoin had traded above $67,000 in November 2021 before collapsing below $20,000 by June 2022, dragging the per-coin realised value well below the capital intensity the company had committed against. Hash rate that year was still sub-scale by later standards—the company had been growing aggressively from its Georgia campus footprint—and the combination of a falling Bitcoin price against rising network difficulty produced the first serious test of the Bradford team's cost discipline.

Fiscal 2023 (ending September 30, 2023) demonstrated the recovery dynamic. Bitcoin stabilised off the FTX-collapse lows around $16,000 in December 2022 and grinded back toward $28,000 by the fiscal year close. Revenue reached approximately $168 million as hash rate scaled materially through that twelve-month window, with new Georgia capacity additions converting megawatt commitments into deployed exahash. The operating loss that had persisted through the crypto-winter trough began narrowing as fleet efficiency improved and electricity contracts renegotiated at lower per-MWh rates reflected the company's growing utility-scale procurement leverage.

| Fiscal Year (Sept 30) | Revenue | Approximate Avg BTC Price (FY Period) | Hash Rate Trajectory |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | ~$116M | ~$35,000 (declining sharply) | Sub-5 EH/s growing |
| FY2023 | ~$168M | ~$22,000 (recovering) | ~5 EH/s → ~8 EH/s |
| FY2024 | >$370M est. | ~$45,000–$65,000 (halving yr) | ~10 EH/s → ~20+ EH/s |

*Sources: CLSK 10-K filings via [SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=CLSK&type=10-K); CleanSpark IR monthly operational updates.*

## The April 2024 Halving: Unit Economics Under the Microscope

The fourth Bitcoin halving on April 20, 2024 cut the per-block subsidy from 6.25 BTC to 3.125 BTC in a single protocol event. The mechanics were known years in advance; the industry response separated operators by electricity cost quartile with unusual clarity. For CleanSpark, the halving landed mid-fiscal year—inside Q3 FY2024 (April through June)—and the company's management had been explicit in the prior quarters that it was preparing operationally rather than hoping for a compensating Bitcoin price rally.

The unit economics calculus shifted materially. Pre-halving, at a network difficulty level prevailing in early 2024 and a Bitcoin price around $60,000, a well-positioned miner running modern S19-series hardware at 3.0–3.5 cents per kilowatt-hour could generate gross margins north of 60% on an all-in cost-to-mine basis. Post-halving at the same electricity rate and hardware vintage, that margin compressed toward 30–35% absent a Bitcoin price appreciation event—which, in the event, did materialise. Bitcoin crossed $73,000 in mid-March 2024 before the halving, retreated, then rebounded through $60,000–$70,000 across the summer of 2024 and surpassed $100,000 by the fourth calendar quarter of that year.

The critical operating variable CleanSpark controlled was its all-in electricity cost. Management had consistently guided toward a sub-4-cent-per-kWh blended rate, citing its Georgia utility relationships and direct grid interconnection arrangements at its principal campus facilities. In the fiscal 2024 10-K and associated earnings commentary, Bradford characterised the company's Georgia footprint as a structural cost advantage, noting that multi-year power purchase agreements locked in capacity at rates below what spot-market-exposed peers faced through the post-halving trough.

> "We entered the halving in the strongest operational position in our history. Our cost structure, our fleet, our power arrangements—we've been building toward this moment for three years."

That operational confidence was underscored by the fleet refresh programme. Through calendar 2023 and into the first half of calendar 2024, CleanSpark executed a progressive migration from the Bitmain Antminer S19-series (28–30 J/TH efficiency range) toward the S21 and S21 Pro generations (17–20 J/TH), with S21 XP units at the leading edge delivering sub-15 J/TH performance. Each efficiency point mattered in the post-halving environment: a 10 J/TH improvement in fleet average translated directly to lower electricity cost per bitcoin produced, offsetting a portion of the reward compression at the protocol level.

## Capital Structure: ATM Equity as the Funding Spine

The mechanism that funded CleanSpark's hash rate scaling was almost entirely equity issuance through successive at-the-market programmes, a model shared with most of its Bitcoin mining peers but pursued by CleanSpark with particular discipline relative to the company's operational delivery. From its S-3 shelf registration filings with the SEC, the company registered multiple ATM facilities across the 2021–2024 period, drawing down hundreds of millions of dollars in aggregate as it funded Georgia campus expansions, ASIC procurement contracts, and working capital through Bitcoin price cycle volatility.

The dilutive cost of that capital was not trivial. Share count grew from approximately 100 million shares outstanding in 2021 toward 230–250 million by fiscal 2024, a compounding dilution that pressed per-share earnings relative to aggregate company economics. Management's defence of the model was consistent: given the absence of long-dated debt markets accessible to Bitcoin miners at reasonable rates, and given the capital intensity of MW-scale data centre buildout, equity issuance was the least-bad funding option through the scaling phase. The implicit bet was that hash rate accumulation and per-coin economics at competitive electricity rates would, at a sufficiently high Bitcoin price, generate operating cash flow adequate to slow ATM dependency.

That crossover arrived, in nascent form, as Bitcoin moved toward and then above $60,000 post-halving. The fiscal 2024 annual results showed operating cash generation sufficient to fund a portion of capex internally, reducing the pace of ATM draws relative to the hyper-scaling years of 2021–2022. The company maintained shelf capacity as an option but characterised its posture as opportunistic rather than necessity-driven.

| ATM / Equity Financing Period | Approximate Shares Issued | Approximate Proceeds | Primary Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2021–2022 | ~60–80M shares | ~$500–700M est. | Campus buildout, ASIC procurement |
| 2023 | ~20–30M shares | ~$150–200M est. | Fleet refresh, expansion |
| 2024 (pre/post halving) | ~15–25M shares | ~$100–175M est. | Capex, working capital |

*Illustrative ranges derived from CLSK S-3, prospectus supplements, and 10-K share count disclosures via [SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=CLSK&type=S-3).*

## The HODL Treasury: Bitcoin on the Balance Sheet

The most consequential capital allocation decision of the post-halving period was the formalisation of CleanSpark's Bitcoin treasury strategy. Through 2022 and 2023, the company had sold a majority of mined Bitcoin into spot markets to fund operations—a common practice among miners whose electricity bills arrived in dollars while revenue was denominated in BTC. As fiscal 2024 progressed and operating cash flow strengthened, Bradford's team shifted posture, retaining a growing portion of daily Bitcoin production.

By late calendar 2024, with Bitcoin approaching and then exceeding $100,000, the decision to accumulate rather than liquidate had produced a balance sheet line that represented both a treasury asset and an ongoing mark-to-market volatility risk. The company disclosed Bitcoin holdings in its quarterly filings, and the aggregate figure grew through successive months of operational production combined with selective retention. The HODL thesis rested on a structural argument: if CleanSpark could fund electricity contracts, ASIC amortisation, and SG&A from operating cash flow, every BTC retained at above-cost prices compounded the treasury position at zero marginal cost.

The accounting treatment evolved concurrently. FASB's updated guidance on digital assets—phasing in fair value measurement for Bitcoin holdings—altered the income statement dynamics for companies like CleanSpark that had previously carried BTC at historical cost less impairment. Under the revised framework, unrealised appreciation would flow through net income, introducing an additional layer of volatility to reported earnings even in quarters where mining operations performed steadily.

## Forward Variables: The Arithmetic of Scale

Through the period leading to the frozen snapshot in May 2026, CleanSpark's financial trajectory was governed by four interacting variables: hash rate scale relative to network difficulty growth, electricity cost per MWh against fleet efficiency, Bitcoin price versus the all-in cost to mine, and the pace of equity dilution required to fund continued scaling.

The network difficulty variable was perhaps the most insidious. Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment mechanism—recalibrating every 2,016 blocks to target a ten-minute average block time—meant that CleanSpark's individual EH/s contribution to network hash rate could remain static while its proportional share of daily block rewards shrank as competing miners added capacity. The post-halving industry consolidation that analysts had anticipated arrived unevenly: some overleveraged operators exited or contracted, while capitalised survivors like CleanSpark, Marathon Digital, and Riot Platforms continued adding exahash, sustaining aggregate network difficulty near record levels even as marginal economics for inefficient operators deteriorated.

CleanSpark's competitive position within that landscape depended on maintaining its electricity cost advantage and sustaining fleet efficiency leadership through ASIC refresh cycles. The capital required for that refresh—S21 XP and next-generation Bitmain hardware—ran to hundreds of dollars per terahash of nameplate capacity, implying hundreds of millions in procurement commitments across the multi-EH/s scaling programme. Whether that capital came from operating cash flow, additional ATM draws, or structured equipment financing depended on Bitcoin price levels that no financial model could confidently assume.

What the company had demonstrated through three fiscal years and a halving event was an operational competence that translated hash rate growth into revenue with minimal execution risk—no meaningful unplanned downtime, no energy contract disputes, no fleet procurement failures that disrupted the cadence of deployed EH/s. The financial story through May 2026 was one of a company that had grown its way into a cost structure defensible at Bitcoin prices well below the levels prevailing at the snapshot date, with a treasury position that rewarded the patience of the scaling investment if Bitcoin price held its post-halving range.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## The Valuation Problem: Pricing a Bitcoin Yield Machine

Valuing a pure-play Bitcoin miner requires confronting an uncomfortable truth: the conventional equity-analysis toolkit fits poorly. CleanSpark produced no product with a stable margin, no recurring software revenue, and no customer contract that survived the next network difficulty adjustment. What it produced was Bitcoin — and its financial results were essentially the product of Bitcoin's price, the network's aggregate hash rate, the company's own share of that hash rate, and the cost structure required to maintain it. This created a valuation framework where every meaningful multiple oscillated with Bitcoin and where terminal value depended on assumptions that were, in any rigorous sense, unforecastable.

That said, markets priced CLSK every day. Understanding how they priced it — and whether that pricing made sense — is the task this chapter undertakes.

## Current Multiple Snapshot

As of the frozen snapshot (May 23, 2026), CleanSpark carried approximately 280–310 million diluted shares outstanding, reflecting the company's sustained reliance on ATM (at-the-money) equity issuance across multiple S-3 shelf facilities filed with the SEC. The FY2024 10-K (fiscal year ended September 30, 2024) reported approximately 265 million diluted shares; continued ATM drawdowns in subsequent quarters pushed the figure higher. With Bitcoin price having moved considerably since the April 2024 halving — trading broadly in the range of $90,000–$115,000 per coin through late CY2025 and into CY2026 — the precise market capitalization remained sensitive to both coin price and share price on any given date. Reasoning from the reported share count range and recent price action, the market capitalization fell in an estimated band of $2.5 billion to $4.5 billion at the frozen snapshot, a range wide enough to carry meaningful analytical uncertainty that readers should weight accordingly.

On reported financials, FY2024 revenue of approximately $378.9 million and a mid-cycle EBITDA figure depressed by the April 2024 halving produced trailing multiples of limited forward utility. Trailing EV/Revenue, on an estimated enterprise value of $2.5–4.0 billion, implied roughly 6–10x — elevated by the standards of industrial operators but consistent with the Bitcoin-option premium embedded across the sector. Trailing P/E was either meaningless in loss-making post-halving quarters or, in Bitcoin-favorable periods, compressed enough to appear cheap on a naive screen.

The forward framework required estimating FY2025 revenue (fiscal year ending September 30, 2025). With hash rate scaling from approximately 28–32 EH/s at FY2024-end toward management's stated 50 EH/s target, and Bitcoin price assumed in a reasonable range consistent with the snapshot window, forward revenue estimates by consensus ranged from approximately $500 million to $800 million for FY2025 depending on Bitcoin price assumptions. On that basis, forward EV/Revenue implied roughly 4–6x — a figure with no natural anchor absent a Bitcoin price view.

## Historical Multiple Range and Re-Rating Dynamics

CleanSpark's multiple history was inseparable from Bitcoin's price cycles. The stock peaked in CY2021 at over $20 per share with a market capitalization exceeding $2 billion at a time when the company was still small in absolute hash-rate terms; the multiple was almost entirely an option premium on future scale and coin appreciation. The 2022 crypto winter compressed the stock to the $3–7 range, with enterprise value briefly threatening to fall below net asset value in the most severe drawdown — implying negative option value for operating leverage at trough.

The recovery through CY2023 and the post-halving bull run of late CY2024 produced a meaningful re-rating as the company demonstrated post-halving operating discipline: hash rate scaled, electricity cost remained competitive, and the fleet refresh toward S21-generation ASICs improved energy efficiency (lower J/TH). At the same time, the ATM equity program continuously diluted the share count, creating a persistent drag on per-share appreciation even as enterprise value grew. The current period was therefore one of partial re-rating: the company had proven it could survive a halving with operating discipline intact, had reached multi-EH/s scale, and had secured power-purchase infrastructure that supported the AI/HPC optionality thesis. But the multiple had not returned to 2021 levels, and the equity dilution overhang from the ATM facilities remained a structural discount factor.

## Peer Group Multiple Comparison

Bitcoin mining multiples were best compared within the sector, where all operators shared the same fundamental Bitcoin-price dependency. The table below compares CleanSpark against its principal peers on the metrics most relevant to the operating model. All figures are estimates based on disclosed hash-rate data, public share counts, and Bitcoin price assumptions consistent with the May 2026 snapshot window; exact figures should be verified against the most recent filings.

| Company | Ticker | Est. Hash Rate (EH/s) | Est. Market Cap ($B) | EV / Fwd Revenue | EV / Fwd EBITDA | EV per EH/s ($M) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CleanSpark | CLSK | ~40–50 | ~$2.5–4.0 | ~4–6x | ~8–14x | ~$60–90 |
| Marathon Digital | MARA | ~45–55 | ~$4.0–7.0 | ~5–8x | ~10–18x | ~$80–130 |
| Riot Platforms | RIOT | ~30–40 | ~$2.5–4.5 | ~4–7x | ~9–15x | ~$70–110 |
| Core Scientific | CORZ | ~15–25 + AI/HPC | ~$5.0–9.0 | ~5–9x | ~12–20x | premium (AI re-rate) |
| Iris Energy | IREN | ~10–20 | ~$1.0–2.5 | ~4–7x | ~9–16x | ~$70–120 |
| TeraWulf | WULF | ~8–15 | ~$0.8–1.8 | ~4–6x | ~8–13x | ~$60–100 |

*Estimates based on publicly available data as of or near the May 2026 frozen snapshot. Figures should be reconciled against the most recent 10-Q and monthly operational updates.*

The most instructive observation was Core Scientific's re-rating premium. Having pivoted aggressively to AI/HPC hosting on its power-secured campus footprint — disclosing definitive customer agreements and revenues from hyperscaler and AI-infrastructure tenants — CORZ commanded a meaningfully higher EV/EH/s and forward-revenue multiple than its pure-play Bitcoin-mining peers. This differential illustrated the AI/HPC optionality premium the market was willing to assign, and implied that CleanSpark's own optionality, if translated into disclosed customer engagements and definitive economics, could trigger a comparable re-rating event.

## Intrinsic Value: What the Current Price Implies

A simplified DCF framework was instructive not for its precision but for the Bitcoin price and margin assumptions it required to close. At a $3 billion enterprise value and a 12% discount rate — a rough risk premium for a Bitcoin-correlated, mid-cap, capital-intensive operator — the market was implicitly pricing in approximately $300–400 million of annual free cash flow in perpetuity on a zero-growth terminal assumption, or lower near-term cash flows with an embedded growth premium.

With FY2025 projected EBITDA in the $150–300 million range (highly sensitive to Bitcoin price), and after subtracting fleet-refresh capex of $100–200 million per year to maintain competitive hash rate against network difficulty growth, sustainable free cash flow was thin under conservative Bitcoin price assumptions and substantial under bull-case assumptions. The current price therefore required either a constructive Bitcoin view or confidence in the AI/HPC pivot delivering higher-margin, less-cyclical revenue to offset mining volatility. There was no price-insensitive DCF case.

## Bull / Base / Bear Valuation Scenarios

**Bull case — Bitcoin at $130,000–$150,000, 50-plus EH/s achieved, AI/HPC optionality realised:** FY2025 revenue approached $900 million–$1.1 billion, EBITDA margins expanded toward 35–40% as efficiency gains from the S21/S21-XP fleet refresh flowed through, and the company announced its first definitive AI/HPC hosting agreement. The market re-rated CleanSpark toward CORZ-like multiples of 10–15x forward EBITDA. The resulting enterprise value implied a stock price in the range of **$18–28 per share** on approximately 300 million diluted shares — representing 100–200% upside from the midpoint of the current range. The AI/HPC re-rating alone, independent of Bitcoin price, could add $3–5 per share in option value.

**Base case — Bitcoin at $90,000–$100,000, 40–45 EH/s, no AI/HPC contract disclosed:** FY2025 revenue of approximately $600–750 million, EBITDA margins of 25–30%, and a pure-play Bitcoin mining multiple of 8–11x forward EBITDA. Enterprise value of roughly $2.5–3.5 billion implied a stock price in the range of **$9–13 per share**. This represented modest upside from current levels but required no re-rating premium — merely execution on disclosed hash-rate targets and cost discipline already demonstrated through the post-halving operating phase.

**Bear case — Bitcoin at $55,000–$65,000, difficulty expansion outpacing hash-rate growth, no AI/HPC traction:** Post-halving economics compressed severely. FY2025 EBITDA fell to $50–100 million as revenue declined toward $350–450 million and the ATM program continued diluting per-share value. At 5–7x compressed EBITDA, enterprise value contracted toward $400–700 million, implying a stock price in the range of **$2–4 per share** — a drawdown consistent with the CY2022 crypto-winter experience and a reminder of the downside asymmetry embedded in a leveraged-to-Bitcoin operating model.

## What the Market Is Pricing In

The current multiple implied a base case roughly centered on $90,000–$100,000 Bitcoin with modest hash-rate scale execution. The market was pricing in operational continuity and no catastrophic dilution, but was not awarding the AI/HPC re-rating premium and was not embedding significant Bitcoin upside. The discount to Core Scientific's multiple was explicit: CLSK was valued as a mining operator, not as a data-center platform, until management converted optionality into disclosed customer revenue and segment economics.

The principal gap between consensus and this dossier's read was on AI/HPC timing. If CleanSpark followed the CORZ or IREN playbook and announced a definitive hosting agreement in the next two to four quarters, the re-rating trigger was already present in the infrastructure: power-secured campus footprint, competent facilities management, and management bandwidth freed by post-halving operating stabilisation. The gap was commercial, not physical. A market pricing CLSK as a pure-play miner was, by definition, pricing that optionality at zero — a conservative assumption that this dossier regarded as the single largest source of upside variance in the stock, and the variable most worth monitoring in the quarters ahead.

chapters.title: Quarterly cadence through halving and hash rate scaling
chapters.body:
## The Bear-Market Foundation: FY2022

CleanSpark's transition into a pure-play Bitcoin miner was stress-tested almost the moment the pivot was complete. The fiscal year ending September 30, 2022, opened on a high — Q1 (December 2021) and Q2 (March 2022) each delivered roughly $41 million in revenue as Bitcoin held above $40,000 — then cracked violently when the market unravelled. Bitcoin fell from above $40,000 toward $18,000 through May and June 2022; Q3 revenue compressed to $31 million and Q4 slid further to $26 million. Full-year revenue reached [$131.5 million](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000827876/000095017022026534/clsk-ex99_1.htm), a near-250 percent increase over the prior year in headline terms — but the back half of the year was effectively a managed retreat. The company reported a net GAAP loss of $57.3 million, with $42.3 million concentrated in Q4 as goodwill and Bitcoin impairment charges compounded operating pressure.

Yet the period exposed what would become the durable logic of the CleanSpark model: hash rate compounded even as revenue halved sequentially. The company exited FY2022 with deployed capacity approaching 5.8 EH/s, more than triple where it had begun the year, funded by a sequence of ATM equity offerings that would become the company's signature capital mechanism. The bear market was not a pause but a construction phase — cheap power contracts were signed, Georgia data centre square footage was absorbed, and the ASIC fleet refreshed. The pain showed in the GAAP income statement; the growth trajectory showed everywhere else.

---

## Expanding Through the Trough: FY2023

The fiscal year that opened October 2022 arrived at the industry's deepest cycle low. Q1 FY2023 (ended December 31, 2022) recorded $27.8 million in revenue — its lowest since the company committed fully to mining — with a GAAP net loss of $29 million and Adjusted EBITDA barely negative at ($1.4 million). The company mined 1,531 bitcoin into a market that was pricing the asset below $17,000. The entire peer group was under existential pressure; several leveraged miners began liquidating ASIC inventories.

CleanSpark did neither. It deployed. Q2 (ended March 2023) revenue recovered to $42.5 million on 1,871 bitcoin mined, with Adjusted EBITDA turning positive at $12.7 million as the network difficulty temporarily softened and BTC began recovering. Q3 pushed further to $45.5 million as operating hashrate crossed 9 EH/s — 135 percent above where the company had begun the fiscal year. The quarterly revenue cadence — [$27.8M → $42.5M → $45.5M → $52.5M](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000827876/000095017023067035/clsk-ex99_1.htm) — traced a straight line of operational momentum. Q4 FY2023 (September 30, 2023) closed at $52.5 million as the company crossed the symbolic 10 EH/s threshold.

Full-year FY2023 revenue reached [$168.4 million](https://investors.cleanspark.com/), up 28 percent from $131.5 million, while annual bitcoin production nearly doubled to 6,903 coins. The GAAP net loss of $137 million reflected non-cash impairment accounting; Adjusted EBITDA recovered to $25 million — proof that the cash economics were functional even at trough Bitcoin prices. The year ended with CleanSpark positioned ahead of nearly every independent miner in hash rate, fleet age, and electricity cost.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue | BTC Mined | Adj. EBITDA | Net Income/(Loss) | Exit Hash Rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | $131.5M | — | $65.7M | ($57.3M) | ~5.8 EH/s |
| FY2023 | $168.4M | 6,903 | $25.0M | ($137.0M) | ~10 EH/s |
| FY2024 | $378.9M | ~7,100 | $245.8M | ($145.8M) | 33.5 EH/s |
| FY2025 | $766.3M | — | — | — | 50+ EH/s |

---

## The Pre-Halving Surge and Halving Test: FY2024

The FY2024 arc broke cleanly into two acts. The first, stretching from October 2023 through March 2024, was the most profitable run in the company's short history. Q1 FY2024 (December 2023) reported $73.8 million in revenue — a 165 percent year-over-year jump — alongside net income of $25.9 million and Adjusted EBITDA of $69.1 million, as Bitcoin's price climbed above $40,000 on spot-ETF anticipation. Operational hashrate crossed 12.5 EH/s. Q2 (March 2024) compressed none of that momentum: $111.8 million in revenue, up 163 percent year-over-year, with net income of $126.7 million driven partly by the sharp Bitcoin price revaluation on Bitcoin holdings. Hashrate breached 17 EH/s — a 60 percent expansion within a single quarter — after the company completed major build-outs at facilities in Mississippi and Georgia.

The second act began at block 840,000. The April 19, 2024 halving cut the block subsidy from 6.25 to 3.125 bitcoin. Q3 FY2024 (ended June 30, 2024) became the crucible. Revenue came in at $104.1 million — still a 129 percent year-over-year gain but a sequential step down from Q2 — and the company mined 1,583 bitcoin across the period, the April print alone reaching 721 coins on the month. Fleet efficiency at the April close stood at 24.22 J/TH against 136,496 deployed units. The next-generation Antminer S21 Pro machines, operating at 15 J/TH, were already arriving.

Bradford framed the moment in the company's April 2024 operational update: the company was "well positioned to excel in this new post-halving environment" while acknowledging that "less efficient miners beginning to cease operations" was the likely near-term dynamic. CFO Gary Vecchiarelli would later be more direct in the full-year results release:

> "Our organizational commitment to operational excellence has allowed us to weather [the halving] more successfully than many of our industry peers."

Hashrate through Q3 crossed 22 EH/s, a 24 percent intra-quarter increase. By Q4 (September 30, 2024) the rate had expanded to more than 33.5 EH/s, with management targeting 37 EH/s by calendar year-end. Total FY2024 production reached approximately 7,100 bitcoin despite the halving's mid-year compression — outpacing both the reward reduction and the network difficulty growth. Full-year revenue of [$378.9 million](https://investors.cleanspark.com/news/news-details/2024/CleanSpark-Reports-Record-Breaking-FY-2024-Results-Outpacing-Halving-and-Difficulty/default.aspx) rose 125 percent year-on-year. Adjusted EBITDA recovered sharply to $245.8 million; the GAAP net loss of $145.8 million ($(0.69) per basic share) reflected non-cash charges. The balance sheet carried $509.5 million of bitcoin (8,049 coins at $63,301 apiece), $122.2 million in cash, and total assets of $2.0 billion — a structurally different company from the one that had navigated the 2022 trough.

> "Our performance this year reflects a sustained growth trajectory, solidifying our position as one of the top Bitcoin miners in the world, as we move into an anticipated new bull market," Bradford stated.

---

## The Breakaway Fiscal Year: FY2025

FY2025 traced the post-halving bull-market scenario that the company had been capitalising for since 2022. Q1 (December 2024) opened with $162.3 million in revenue — up 120 percent year-over-year — and net income of $246.8 million, or $0.85 per basic share. Fleet efficiency had compressed from the 24.22 J/TH of the April halving month to 16.15 J/TH by December, a 33 percent improvement in eight months as S21 Pro machines filled the data centres. Marginal cost to mine sat near $34,000 per bitcoin against a spot price well above $90,000; gross margin reached 57 percent.

Q2 (March 2025) produced $181.7 million in revenue — 1,957 bitcoin mined at an average realised price of $92,811 per coin — as hashrate exceeded 40 EH/s. Q3 (June 2025) delivered $198.6 million in revenue, up 91 percent year-over-year, with net income of $257.4 million and Adjusted EBITDA of $377.7 million. Bitcoin treasury stood at 12,703 coins valued at approximately $1.08 billion. In June 2025, CleanSpark reached 50 EH/s of operational capacity, representing roughly 5.8 percent of the global network — the first public miner to achieve that threshold built exclusively on American infrastructure. Power under contract crossed one gigawatt.

Bradford's characterisation for Q3 FY2025 set the tone for what management saw as a pivotal transition:

> "This was the most successful quarter in CleanSpark's history, and it reflects the strength of our strategy, the discipline of our execution, and the tireless commitment of our team."

CFO Vecchiarelli's framing of the same quarter underscored the treasury accumulation discipline: "Fiscal Q3 was a pivotal quarter for CleanSpark, as we fully funded operational expenses through monthly bitcoin production while simultaneously expanding our bitcoin treasury."

Full-year FY2025 revenue reached [$766.3 million](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000827876/000119312525297163/clsk-ex99_1.htm), a 102 percent year-on-year gain and more than five-and-a-half times the FY2022 base. That same November 2025 announcement accompanied the disclosure of a landmark $1.15 billion aggregate principal of 0.00 percent Convertible Senior Notes due 2032 — a transaction that closed November 13, 2025 — with proceeds directed toward power and land portfolio expansion, data centre infrastructure, and repayment of bitcoin-backed credit balances. The instrument, carrying a 27.5 percent conversion premium, was designed to buy optionality on what management described as the company's evolution into "a comprehensive compute platform prepared to optimize value from both AI and bitcoin workloads."

The four-year revenue arc — $131.5M, $168.4M, $378.9M, $766.3M — mapped almost precisely to a hash rate arc of 5.8, 10-plus, 33.5, and 50-plus EH/s. The correlation was the point. Every dollar of ATM equity issued in the 2022-2023 bear market funded the megawatt capacity that drove the 2024-2025 revenue. The Bitcoin halving, which the industry dreaded as a margin-compressor, arrived at CleanSpark as a hash rate scale advantage: the company's capital-light legacy fleet was being retired just as the fixed-cost base expanded, and by the time the new block subsidy regime had settled, CleanSpark held more productive capacity — and more bitcoin — than at any prior moment in its history.

chapters.title: Zach Bradford, CFO, executive team, and the board
chapters.body:
## The architect: Bradford's decade at the helm

The CleanSpark that arrived at the April 2024 Bitcoin halving — multi-EH/s, debt-light, and operating across five states — was substantially the creation of one person's sustained managerial will. Zachary K. Bradford co-founded the company alongside S. Matthew Schultz in March 2014 as a twenty-something certified public accountant whose formal credentials were, at that point, a Bachelor of Science in accounting and a Master of Accountancy from Southern Utah University, completed in 2011 and 2012 respectively, and a Henderson, Nevada public accounting and consulting practice he had established the previous year. Bradford was elected Chief Financial Officer at founding, and for five years he ran the company's finances through its biomass-energy and renewable-energy-software phases — periods of minimal revenue and near-constant capital stress — before the board elevated him to Chief Executive Officer in October 2019, just as the Bitcoin mining pivot was beginning in earnest.

The transition from CFO to CEO was not, in the conventional corporate sense, a promotion across a functional divide. Bradford's instincts remained those of a cost accountant: unit economics, capital efficiency, and the relationship between energy input and revenue output. Those instincts proved unusually well-suited to an industry where the margin between profit and loss is measured in joules per terahash. In investor presentations and earnings calls across 2022, 2023, and 2024, Bradford returned repeatedly to a single theme.

> "Efficiency is the most important variable as we head into the halving."

He was, as events proved, right. The company entered the post-halving environment having systematically retired older-generation ASIC hardware in favour of Bitmain's S21 and S21 XP series, achieving what Bradford described as having "cemented our lead as the most efficient publicly traded bitcoin miner at scale in North America." The fleet refresh was not incidental; it was the operational expression of an accountant's recognition that when revenue per coin is halved by protocol fiat, only a lower cost structure preserves the margin.

Bradford's tenure produced measurable results. Under his leadership CleanSpark expanded from a single pilot facility to a portfolio spanning Georgia, Mississippi, Wyoming, New York, Tennessee, and beyond, with more than 750 megawatts of capacity and approximately 300 employees at peak. He guided more than a dozen acquisitions, oversaw the company's transition from OTC markets to Nasdaq, and — alongside CFO Gary Vecchiarelli — accessed equity capital markets repeatedly through at-the-market facilities to fund hash-rate growth without taking on the project-finance leverage that encumbered several peers.

> "CleanSpark has prioritized owned infrastructure as its core foundation, putting us in the best position to optimize our portfolio of data centers."

On 10 August 2025, Bradford resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and director, effective immediately. In a departure statement he cited a personal imperative rather than any strategic rupture: "The time has come for me to transition the role to the next leader and focus on my family. I am confident in the bright future ahead." The board accepted the resignation, reduced its size from six members to five, and asked co-founder Schultz — who had relinquished the CEO title to Bradford in October 2019 and served as Executive Chairman in the intervening years — to resume operational command.

## The co-founder's return: Matt Schultz as chief executive

S. Matthew Schultz, age 55 at the time of the proxy filing, had been present at every consequential inflection in CleanSpark's history. He led the biomass-energy phase, oversaw the pivot to renewable-energy software, and was instrumental in the early capital raises that provided the liquidity base for the Bitcoin mining build-out — by his own count, more than $3.8 billion in capital raised across his tenures as CEO and as Executive Chairman. His return to the chief executive seat in August 2025 was framed not as a strategic reorientation but as continuity under a founder's hand. "My focus stepping in as CEO is to ensure stability, continuity, and forward momentum during this time," Schultz stated at the announcement. The board indicated that existing management priorities and strategic plans would remain unchanged.

By the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, Schultz was heading a leadership team assembled largely during Bradford's tenure and largely intact through the transition.

## The finance function: Vecchiarelli as CFO and President

Gary A. Vecchiarelli joined CleanSpark as Chief Financial Officer in December 2021 and had, by the snapshot date, accumulated the additional title of President, reflecting an expansion of his mandate beyond the purely financial. He was 47 at the time of the fiscal 2025 proxy, held a bachelor's degree in business administration and accounting from California State University, San Jose, and carried an active CPA licence in both California and Nevada dating to 2006. His career before CleanSpark moved through the gaming and hospitality verticals that define Las Vegas's public-company ecosystem: audit manager at BDO USA's Las Vegas practice, finance leadership at Galaxy Gaming, and Chief Financial Officer roles at Golden Entertainment and subsequently at Imatrex, a medical-imaging company.

At CleanSpark, Vecchiarelli's fingerprints are most legible on the capital-markets activities: the design and execution of successive ATM equity offerings, the structuring of acquisition financing, and the management of a balance-sheet that by late 2024 held nearly $700 million in cash and Bitcoin with effectively no funded debt. The [fiscal year 2025 proxy](https://d18rn0p25nwr6d.cloudfront.net/CIK-0000827876/b89f279c-c0d0-4689-b3bf-a5761d6851cb.html) credited him with being "instrumental in building the strong balance sheet enabling it to become one of the largest corporate holders of bitcoin."

## The operating tier: Garrison, Monnig, and the specialist layer

The senior management bench that Schultz inherited was populated with operators whose résumés spanned mining infrastructure, immersion cooling, and defence-sector project management. Scott Garrison, Chief Development Officer and Executive Vice President, had spent more than three decades in technology, software, hospitality, and media infrastructure before joining CleanSpark in November 2020 as Senior Vice President of Growth. He founded and operated two technology consultancies — Linq360 and The Integration Center — and provided advisory services to Hewlett-Packard, Verizon, Microsoft, and Samsung before turning his attention to Bitcoin mining. By 2024 he had led the development and optimisation of more than 700 megawatts of CleanSpark infrastructure across the country.

Taylor Monnig, Chief Operating Officer and Chief Technology Officer, was 32 at the time of the proxy and brought with him the credentialled background of someone who had already built and scaled a competing hardware company. He was the COO of TMGCore from April 2018 to August 2022, developing single-phase and two-phase immersion-cooling systems for both high-performance computing and Bitcoin mining — and holds patents in data-centre cooling technology, alongside an Intel innovation award. His promotion to CTO, formalised on 7 May 2024, came just weeks before the halving; his subsequent expansion into the COO remit reflected the company's increasing integration of operational and technological functions.

Brian Carson, Chief Accounting Officer, brought more than three decades of corporate accounting and financial-planning experience, including time as financial controller at SAHARA Las Vegas and as an audit manager at Deloitte. Harry Sudock, Chief Business Officer, was SVP and Chief Strategy Officer at GRIID Infrastructure before joining CleanSpark, having been that company's first employee in 2018 and carrying responsibility for investor relations and strategic communications. Leighton Koehler, General Counsel, served previously as general counsel for Planet 13 Holdings and holds both a law licence and CPA certification in Nevada; he is also a veteran of the United States Army.

## The board: four independents around a founder-chairman

At the frozen snapshot date, the CleanSpark board comprised five members: Schultz as non-independent Chairman and CEO, and four independent directors whose collective tenures and specialisations provided the governance architecture around which the company conducted its audit, compensation, and nominating functions.

| Director | Role | Since | Background |
|---|---|---|---|
| S. Matthew Schultz | Chairman & CEO | Mar 2014 | Co-founder; energy and Bitcoin mining |
| Larry McNeill | Lead Independent Director | Jan 2015 | SVP Corporate Development, Smith's Food & Drug; retail finance |
| Roger P. Beynon | Director | Oct 2019 | CPA, CFE; founder, Beynon & Associates (40 years); audit committee financial expert |
| Dr. Thomas L. Wood | Director | Oct 2019 | U.S. Navy civil engineering; ~$1 bn annual Pacific Engineering Command contracts; PE; DBA |
| Amanda Cavaleri | Director | Dec 2022 | Bitcoin mining operator; Bitcoin advisory; co-author, *Bitcoin and the American Dream* |

Larry McNeill, Lead Independent Director since October 2024 and the board's longest-serving independent voice, joined in January 2015 at an age — then 72, by the snapshot date 83 — that makes him an institutional memory running back to the company's earliest corporate iterations. His background in retail-sector corporate development, spanning A&P, Safeway's European and Australian expansion programmes, and seventeen years as Senior Vice President of Corporate Development at Smith's Food and Drug Stores, gave him the financial-governance grounding that the audit committee chair role demands.

Roger Beynon, who chairs the Audit Committee and carries an "audit committee financial expert" designation under Nasdaq standards, founded his Utah-based public accounting and forensic practice in 1984 and has run it for more than four decades. Thomas Wood brings a civil-engineering and defence-acquisition background — thirty-nine years in planning, operations, and construction management, rising to Deputy Operations for the U.S. Navy's Pacific Engineering Command with oversight of approximately $1 billion in annual contracts — that informs the board's oversight of the company's capital-intensive infrastructure build-out programme. Amanda Cavaleri, the youngest and most recently appointed independent, is a practitioner rather than an observer: she operated a Wyoming Bitcoin mining site as CEO from October 2021 to November 2024, advises hedge funds and venture funds through a Bitcoin ecosystem advisory practice, and chairs the Bitcoin Today Coalition.

Independent directors received a total annual package of $320,000 in fiscal year 2024, comprising a $120,000 cash retainer and $200,000 in restricted-stock units vesting at 25% per quarter. The board met sixteen times in fiscal year 2024, with all directors recording attendance above the 75% threshold required under Nasdaq rules.

The governance posture — a founder-chairman in the CEO seat, a financially credentialled independent lead director, and a newly refreshed independent cohort with direct Bitcoin mining and engineering exposure — reflected the company's self-description as an infrastructure and energy business that happens to mine Bitcoin, rather than a speculative digital-asset vehicle. Whether that characterisation survived contact with the AI/HPC pivot optionality thesis, and what executive talent it might require to execute, remained one of the unresolved questions hanging over the team as of the snapshot date.
