chapters.title: Bitcoin protocol mining and potential AI/HPC hosting customers
chapters.body:
## The Protocol as Customer: Mining Economics at Scale

CleanSpark operates without a conventional customer base. Its sole "buyer" is the Bitcoin network itself — the decentralized protocol that, since the fourth halving event of April 19, 2024, awards a miner 3.125 BTC for every valid block appended to the chain roughly every ten minutes. That single architectural fact defines the company's commercial model entirely: maximize hash rate deployed, minimize all-in electricity cost per terahash, maintain fleet efficiency at the leading edge of the ASIC technology curve, and convert the resulting Bitcoin production into revenue through institutional trading channels.

The April 2024 halving compressed industry-wide unit economics with surgical precision. Block rewards fell from 6.25 BTC to 3.125 BTC in a single event, cutting gross revenue per block in half at any given Bitcoin price. Miners carrying older, power-hungry hardware — particularly S19-generation ASICs running at 29–35 joules per terahash — faced immediate margin compression. At network difficulty levels prevailing through mid-2024, the breakeven electricity cost for such machines fell toward or below the all-in procurement price achievable by all but the most favorably positioned operators. Bradford had anticipated the constraint. Speaking to the post-halving environment on CleanSpark's earnings calls through fiscal year 2024, the CEO repeatedly framed energy procurement and fleet modernization as the company's primary competitive variables — not market share in a customer sense, but hash rate share captured at defensible unit economics.

## Monetizing the Output: Coinbase Prime and the Institutional OTC Market

Bitcoin produced by CleanSpark's ASIC fleet is transferred from the mining pool and sold through institutional channels, principally [Coinbase Prime](https://prime.coinbase.com/) — the prime brokerage arm of Coinbase Global — supplemented by OTC trading desks capable of handling block-sized Bitcoin liquidations without material market impact. The company has historically adopted a dynamic Bitcoin treasury management posture, calibrating disposition between daily operational requirements, capital expenditure cadence, and management's near-term price view, rather than operating as either a pure daily-sell or unconstrained accumulation vehicle.

This is a narrow counterparty set by design. Bitcoin's global OTC infrastructure is deep relative to CleanSpark's daily production volume; the company's hash rate, even at multi-EH/s scale, represents a fraction of daily Bitcoin issuance at the network level. Coinbase Prime, NYDIG, FalconX, and comparable institutional desks collectively absorb miner production across the industry without meaningful price discovery impact for any single operator. CleanSpark's counterparty concentration risk, in the traditional corporate finance sense, is therefore not a material operational constraint.

[Monthly operational updates](https://investors.cleanspark.com/) published through CleanSpark's investor relations portal disclosed Bitcoin production figures alongside beginning and end-of-period treasury balances, allowing analysts to track net liquidation patterns against the prevailing spot price. Through fiscal year 2024, the company maintained a meaningful Bitcoin balance on its balance sheet, reflecting both operational timing and an intermittent accumulation posture during periods when management judged spot prices to be below intrinsic value.

## Hash Rate Scaling and the Efficiency Imperative

The commercial logic of Bitcoin mining reduces, in compressed form, to a race between the operator's marginal cost per terahash-second and the network's difficulty-adjusted revenue per terahash-second. CleanSpark's response to the post-halving environment was to accelerate, not defer, fleet modernization. The company executed multi-tranche procurement of Bitmain Antminer S21 Pro and S21 XP generation machines through 2024 and into 2025, displacing older S19-series hardware running at substantially higher joules per terahash.

| ASIC Generation | Nominal Efficiency (J/TH) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Bitmain S19j Pro | ~29.5 | Pre-2023 fleet baseline |
| Bitmain S21 | ~17.5 | 2024 fleet refresh entry-point |
| Bitmain S21 Pro | ~15.0 | High-efficiency 2024 standard |
| Bitmain S21 XP | ~13.5 | Leading-edge 2024–2025 deployment |

The S21 XP generation represents a step-function improvement over the S19j Pro — a gap that translates directly into electricity cost per Bitcoin mined at any given network difficulty. At an all-in electricity cost of $30/MWh, the difference between running 29.5 J/TH hardware and 13.5 J/TH hardware narrows or eliminates positive cash margins for older machines at post-halving block rewards; newer machines retain operating profitability through a substantially wider price and difficulty band. Fleet refresh was therefore not a discretionary optimization but a structural requirement for remaining in the market.

CleanSpark's hash rate trajectory through fiscal year 2025 reflected the combined effect of fleet refresh and facility expansion. The company had articulated targets toward 50 EH/s of operational capacity — a threshold that would place it among the largest pure-play Bitcoin miners by deployed hash rate. Its facilities in Georgia anchored the production base, with supplemental data centers in Mississippi, Tennessee, Wyoming, and New York providing geographic and regulatory diversification.

## The Peer Landscape: Consolidation and the AI/HPC Fork in the Road

The post-halving competitive environment accelerated a strategic bifurcation across the listed Bitcoin mining sector. A subset of operators moved aggressively to repurpose power-secured campus capacity toward AI/HPC hosting. [Core Scientific](https://investors.corescientific.com/) (CORZ) executed the sector's canonical reference transaction — a multi-hundred-megawatt, multi-year hosting agreement with CoreWeave (CRWV), announced in 2023 and expanded through 2024, that repositioned the company from distressed Bitcoin miner to high-value AI infrastructure host. [Iris Energy](https://ir.irisenergy.co/) (IREN) built out GPU cloud capacity alongside its Bitcoin mining operations. [TeraWulf](https://www.terawulf.com/investors/) (WULF) pursued AI hosting buildout at its Lake Mariner facility in upstate New York. Hut 8 (HUT) restructured around a diversified compute platform. The pattern was consistent: operators with power delivery infrastructure and favorable long-term site agreements could offer AI/HPC customers something in acute shortage — reliable, large-scale electricity at the grid edge, delivered under long-term contractual terms.

| Peer | Primary Revenue Posture (as of 2025) | AI/HPC Pivot Status |
|---|---|---|
| Core Scientific (CORZ) | AI/HPC hosting + Bitcoin mining | Executed; CoreWeave anchor contract |
| Iris Energy (IREN) | Bitcoin mining + AI compute | Active; GPU cloud and HPC buildout |
| TeraWulf (WULF) | Bitcoin mining + AI hosting | Active; Lake Mariner AI conversion |
| Hut 8 (HUT) | Diversified compute + Bitcoin | Active; managed services and HPC |
| Marathon Digital (MARA) | Pure-play Bitcoin mining | Limited; primarily Bitcoin-focused |
| Riot Platforms (RIOT) | Pure-play Bitcoin mining | Limited; primarily Bitcoin-focused |
| **CleanSpark (CLSK)** | **Pure-play Bitcoin mining** | **Optionality under active evaluation** |

Bradford's public posture through this period emphasized discipline over opportunism. The CEO consistently positioned CleanSpark as a Bitcoin-first operator whose competitive advantage derived from energy procurement, fleet efficiency, and operational execution rather than from rapid reorientation toward AI hosting. The framing was deliberate: in a sector where the "AI pivot" narrative had become a default capital markets positioning regardless of operational readiness, CleanSpark sought differentiation through demonstrated Bitcoin mining unit economics — a stance with strategic credibility given the company's sustained hash rate growth and cost discipline through the halving cycle.

## AI/HPC Optionality: The Power Asset as Strategic Currency

That discipline did not, however, foreclose the optionality conversation. CleanSpark's owned and long-term-leased data center facilities represent significant interconnected power capacity — grid connections, substation infrastructure, and cooling plant that are, in principle, fungible between Bitcoin ASIC deployment and GPU or accelerator cluster hosting. The economics of that fungibility depend on several variables: the power density profile of the target workload, the cooling infrastructure configuration, the term structure of underlying land and power agreements, and the customer credit quality achievable in AI/HPC hosting markets.

The potential customer set for any CleanSpark AI/HPC hosting offering would span three broad categories. Hyperscalers — Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, Meta — have demonstrated willingness to underwrite long-duration data center leases against their own AI infrastructure capacity planning. AI pure-plays such as CoreWeave (CRWV), Nebius (NBIS), and Lambda Labs actively seek power-secured capacity to deploy proprietary GPU clusters under managed service or colocation arrangements. Enterprise AI customers requiring dedicated compute environments represent a third, smaller category with shorter-duration and more modest-scale requirements.

The challenge for CleanSpark, relative to peers who had already executed AI/HPC hosting transactions, was one of infrastructure configuration and conversion economics. Bitcoin mining facilities optimized for S21-generation ASIC density differ materially from GPU cluster hosting environments: power density per rack, cooling architecture, physical security requirements, network connectivity specifications, and revenue per megawatt achievable vary substantially across the two workloads. A facility generating a given monthly revenue per megawatt in Bitcoin mining at prevailing BTC price and network difficulty must clear a credible AI/HPC revenue hurdle — factoring in conversion capital expenditure and any stranded fleet value — before the switch makes economic sense. At the Bitcoin price levels prevailing through 2024 and 2025, and given CleanSpark's efficiency-leading fleet, the hurdle rate for conversion was non-trivial.

Management's commentary through the period acknowledged the optionality without committing to specific conversion timelines or disclosed customer engagements. The company's geographically distributed power portfolio — spanning Georgia, Mississippi, Tennessee, Wyoming, and New York — provided the raw material for differentiated product offerings to AI/HPC customers with state-specific preferences on regulatory environment, renewable energy profile, or network latency. Whether CleanSpark would elect to exercise that optionality in a material way, or sustain its pure-play Bitcoin mining identity through the next difficulty and price cycle, remained the defining forward strategic question as of the frozen snapshot date.

chapters.title: Where CLSK sits against RIOT, MARA, CORZ, IREN, WULF, BITF, HUT, BTDR
chapters.body:
Within the cohort of publicly traded Bitcoin miners, CleanSpark occupied an unambiguous third-place position in the global hash rate hierarchy as of early 2026. It sat behind Marathon Digital Holdings (MARA), which reported an energised hash rate of approximately 66.4 exahashes per second (EH/s) at 31 December 2025, and Bitdeer Technologies (BTDR), whose self-mining capacity surged to 65.5 EH/s by early 2026 — a 428 percent year-over-year increase driven by rapid deployment of its proprietary SEALMINER A2 and A3 ASICs. CleanSpark's own [December 2025 operational update](https://investors.cleanspark.com/news/news-details/2026/CleanSpark-Releases-December-2025-Bitcoin-Mining-Update/default.aspx) confirmed 50.0 EH/s operational and an average operating rate of 47.2 EH/s, with 245,199 deployed miners consuming 808 megawatts across 1.45 gigawatts of contracted power. That placed CleanSpark ahead of Riot Platforms (RIOT), whose average operating hash rate ran at 36.4 EH/s through Q1 2026, and ahead of Iris Energy (IREN) at approximately 36.0 EH/s, confirming CleanSpark as the largest self-operated, US-domiciled Bitcoin miner in the pure-play category.

## The Scale Hierarchy

The eight-company peer set stratifies into three tiers. At the top, MARA and BTDR compete on raw exahash volume, each having crossed 60 EH/s by early 2026. MARA built its lead through an aggressive acquisition and hosting strategy across the United States and internationally, accumulating 44,893 BTC by year-end 2025 through a modified HODL approach. BTDR's ascent was more structurally distinctive: the Singapore-based operator developed an in-house ASIC programme culminating in the SEALMINER A3 series, with the next-generation SEAL04 chip targeting 6–7 joules per terahash (J/TH) at the chip level in low-voltage mode — a specification that, if realised at scale, would represent the frontier of fleet efficiency among public miners. The speed of BTDR's hash rate expansion — from under 15 EH/s in late 2024 to more than 65 EH/s by early 2026 — reflected vertical integration into silicon manufacturing, a structural differentiation that no other peer in the cohort had replicated.

CleanSpark and Riot competed in the second tier. [Riot's Q1 2026 results](https://www.riotplatforms.com/riot-platforms-reports-first-quarter-2026-financial-results-and-strategic-highlights/) showed a deployed hash rate of 42.5 EH/s at quarter-end, against CleanSpark's installed 50 EH/s — a gap of roughly 7–8 EH/s in CleanSpark's favour. Bitfarms (BITF) and Iris Energy occupied a third tier at roughly 19–36 EH/s, while TeraWulf (WULF) and Core Scientific (CORZ) operated below 20 EH/s as each executed deliberate pivots away from Bitcoin mining economics and toward higher-margin AI and high-performance compute (HPC) hosting.

| Company | Operating Hash Rate | Fleet Efficiency | Contracted Power | Strategic Posture |
|---------|--------------------|--------------------|------------------|--------------------|
| MARA | ~66–72 EH/s | Not disclosed | Global multi-site | BTC treasury + mining scale |
| BTDR | ~65 EH/s | SEAL04 target: 6–7 J/TH | ~570 MW (Ohio) + Malaysia | Vertical ASIC manufacturing |
| CLSK | ~50 EH/s | **16.07 J/TH** | **1.45 GW** | Pure-play + AI optionality |
| RIOT | ~36–42 EH/s | 20.2 J/TH | 2.0 GW approved | Mining + data-centre hosting |
| IREN | ~36–50 EH/s | Not disclosed | 660 MW operating | Aggressive AI cloud pivot |
| BITF | ~19.5 EH/s | 19 J/TH | US/Canada | Defensive consolidation |
| CORZ | ~15.7 EH/s (declining) | Not disclosed | 1.5 GW pipeline | Full AI/HPC conversion |
| WULF | ~12.8 EH/s | Not disclosed | ~245 MW + pipeline | Nuclear anchor + HPC hosting |
| HUT | ~27 EH/s (via ABTC spinoff) | 20.1 J/TH | 1 GW+ pipeline | AI campus build-out |

## The Cost and Efficiency Axis

Beyond raw scale, the post-halving period since April 2024 fused two variables into a single survival test: fleet efficiency (joules per terahash) and all-in energy cost (dollars per kilowatt-hour). CleanSpark entered the comparison with a fleet-average efficiency of 16.07 J/TH by December 2025, reflecting systematic deployment of Bitmain Antminer S21 Pro and S21 XP generation hardware. Against Riot's reported 20.2 J/TH in Q1 2026, CleanSpark's roughly 4 joule-per-terahash advantage translated directly into lower electricity consumption per unit of hash rate — a durable edge on the per-coin operating cost line. Both companies arrived at a similar reported cost-to-mine figure: CleanSpark cited approximately $44,806 per bitcoin in its third fiscal quarter of 2025, while Riot reported $44,629 per coin (excluding depreciation) for Q1 2026.

The energy cost comparison was more nuanced. [Riot's Q1 2026 earnings release](https://www.riotplatforms.com/riot-platforms-reports-first-quarter-2026-financial-results-and-strategic-highlights/) disclosed an all-in power cost of $0.030 per kilowatt-hour after $21 million in power curtailment credits earned at its Rockdale and Corsicana facilities in Texas — a structural benefit flowing from Riot's 2.0 gigawatts of utility-approved capacity and its ability to sell demand reductions back to the ERCOT grid during peak periods. CleanSpark's $0.056 per kilowatt-hour reflected blended rates across its Georgia, Mississippi, Tennessee, Wyoming and New York facilities without equivalent curtailment optionality at current scale. The gap was real but context-dependent: Riot's net curtailment revenue of $21 million in a single quarter represented an operational variable with both upside and downside — a cost that could widen or narrow with grid conditions — while CleanSpark's contracted PPA portfolio offered greater rate stability across Bitcoin price cycles.

## The Pivot Spectrum: Converts, Opportunists, and Holdouts

The sharpest strategic fault line in the cohort ran between operators who treated Bitcoin mining as a legacy cashflow business being harvested to fund AI/HPC buildouts, and those who maintained mining as the primary growth vector.

Core Scientific stood at the committed end of the spectrum. Emerging from Chapter 11 bankruptcy in December 2023 with a restructured balance sheet, CORZ redirected its infrastructure toward AI/HPC colocation, executing a 270-megawatt hosting agreement with CoreWeave and citing a development pipeline of over 1.5 gigawatts of leasable AI capacity. Its self-mining hash rate fell to approximately 15.7 EH/s by early 2026 as miners were decommissioned and repurposed space handed to hyperscale tenants. Management described potential cumulative revenue with CoreWeave exceeding $10 billion over the life of the contracts. In April 2026, the company priced $3.3 billion of senior secured notes to fund continued campus development, cementing its identity as an AI infrastructure operator that happened to retain residual Bitcoin mining.

Iris Energy and Hut 8 had executed pivots of comparable magnitude but from different starting positions. IREN reached 50 EH/s of Bitcoin mining capacity in the first half of 2025, simultaneously building AI cloud infrastructure on the same power-secured campuses. By May 2026, the company disclosed a $3.4 billion AI cloud contract and a five-gigawatt strategic partnership with NVIDIA, targeting $3.7 billion in annualised run-rate AI Cloud revenue and expansion toward 1.2 gigawatts of AI Cloud capacity by 2027 — positioning that effectively reclassified IREN from a Bitcoin miner with AI optionality into an AI infrastructure operator with Bitcoin mining on the side. Hut 8 executed a structural separation: its Bitcoin mining operations were transferred into American Bitcoin (ABTC), a vehicle with approximately 25 EH/s of mining capacity, while the parent retained power rights and site control, signing a 15-year, 352-megawatt IT lease at its Beacon Point AI campus with a base-term contract value of $9.8 billion, plus a $7 billion, 245-megawatt Google-backed agreement at its River Bend, Louisiana site.

TeraWulf occupied a distinct niche. With roughly 12.8 EH/s of Bitcoin mining hash rate — the smallest of any major US peer — WULF's competitive identity rested on its Lake Anna, Virginia nuclear-power-adjacent campus providing structural energy cost advantages, and on its Fluidstack AI hosting agreements signed in August 2025, backstopped by Google to a value of $1.8 billion and supplemented by a 168-megawatt, 25-year joint venture lease representing approximately $9.5 billion in contracted revenue. HPC lease revenue contributed $21 million of WULF's $34 million Q1 2026 total, with the company carrying approximately $3.1 billion of cash and restricted cash at quarter-end.

Bitfarms stood apart as a deliberate holdout from both the scale race and the pivot. Following the acquisition of Stronghold Digital Mining, the sale of its Yguazu, Paraguay facility, and a subsequent exit from all Latin American operations by January 2026, BITF consolidated to a North American-focused fleet of roughly 19.5 EH/s at 19 J/TH efficiency. Management announced no large miner purchases for 2025 or 2026, absorbing a 20 percent reduction in planned capital expenditure — a posture that read as prudent capital preservation but that also conceded ground in the hash rate race to better-capitalised peers.

## CleanSpark's Differentiated Positioning

Against this landscape, CleanSpark maintained the most disciplined pure-play positioning of any company at significant scale. Its [FY2025 results](https://investors.cleanspark.com/news/news-details/2025/CleanSpark-Reports-Transformative-FY-2025-Results/default.aspx) — $766.3 million in revenue, $364.5 million net income, and adjusted EBITDA of $823.4 million — demonstrated that post-halving operating leverage was achievable at 50 EH/s with sufficient fleet efficiency and PPA discipline. The company exited fiscal 2025 holding 13,099 BTC and carrying $644.6 million in long-term debt, the latter dominated by a $1.15 billion zero-coupon convertible note issued in November 2025 with proceeds partly redeployed into a 271-acre, 285-megawatt site acquisition in Austin County, Texas — its [first explicit AI/HPC positioning move](https://investors.cleanspark.com/news/news-details/2025/CleanSpark-Enters-Texas-Market-with-Land-and-Large-Scale-Power-Acquisition-to-Rapidly-Deploy-an-AI-Data-Center-in-Greater-Houston/default.aspx), targeting phased energisation for AI workloads starting mid-2027.

> "Fiscal 2025 was the year CleanSpark achieved operating leverage…We are evolving into a comprehensive compute platform." — CEO Zach Bradford, FY2025 Earnings

The crucial distinction was sequencing. Where CORZ, IREN, and HUT had committed to AI/HPC at the cost of Bitcoin mining market share, CleanSpark preserved mining primacy while accumulating the power and land assets required for an AI pivot. The 50 EH/s base — achieved, per the company, as the first publicly traded Bitcoin miner to reach that threshold with fully self-operated data centres — gave it a volume foundation that smaller AI-pivoting peers had surrendered. The 16.07 J/TH fleet efficiency placed it ahead of RIOT and BITF on the cost curve, while Riot's curtailment-credit-adjusted $0.030/kWh power cost remained the more aggressively structured energy position in the US cohort. MARA's larger raw scale carried the caveat of more complex, geographically dispersed operations; BTDR's chip-manufacturing moat represented the most differentiated long-term threat if SEAL04 production economics translated to the operational fleet. Against that field, CleanSpark's positioning through the frozen window — largest pure-play US self-operator, third in global hash rate, carrying a 1.45-gigawatt contracted power portfolio and an unfunded but option-preserved AI footprint in Texas — reflected a strategy of keeping both futures open until the market made clear which would price at a premium.

---

**Sources:** [CleanSpark December 2025 Operational Update](https://investors.cleanspark.com/news/news-details/2026/CleanSpark-Releases-December-2025-Bitcoin-Mining-Update/default.aspx) · [CleanSpark FY2025 Results](https://investors.cleanspark.com/news/news-details/2025/CleanSpark-Reports-Transformative-FY-2025-Results/default.aspx) · [CleanSpark Texas Acquisition](https://investors.cleanspark.com/news/news-details/2025/CleanSpark-Enters-Texas-Market-with-Land-and-Large-Scale-Power-Acquisition-to-Rapidly-Deploy-an-AI-Data-Center-in-Greater-Houston/default.aspx) · [Riot Q1 2026 Earnings](https://www.riotplatforms.com/riot-platforms-reports-first-quarter-2026-financial-results-and-strategic-highlights/) · [Bitcoin Miners Hashrate Ranking](https://bitcoinminingstock.io/hashrate) · [MARA September 2025 Update](https://ir.mara.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/1410/mara-announces-bitcoin-production-and-mining-operation-updates-forseptember-2025) · [Core Scientific CoreWeave Press Release](https://investors.corescientific.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/9/core-scientific-to-provide-coreweave-up-to-16-mw-of-data-center-infrastructure-to-support-ai-and-hpc-workloads-in-long-term-hosting-contract-with-potential-revenue-of-more-than-100-million) · [Hut 8 AI Campus](https://www.hut8.com/2025/04/04/hut-8-operations-update-for-march-2025/) · [CleanSpark 50 EH/s Milestone](https://www.cleanspark.com/blog/bitcoin-com-news-cleanspark-sets-ambitious-new-hashrate-target-after-reaching-30-eh-s/)

chapters.title: Timeline from energy-software era through Bitcoin mining pivot to 2024-2026
chapters.body:
## From Microgrid Software to Mining Giant

The corporate entity that would become CleanSpark was incorporated on **October 15, 1987**, as SmartData Corporation — a technology company whose original operations were suspended by 1992. The shell re-emerged as Stratean, Inc. in 2014, pursuing gasification technology and distributed energy software. On July 7, 2016, Stratean announced the acquisition of CleanSpark, LLC, a provider of distributed energy resource management systems and microgrid engineering controls, in an all-equity transaction valued at approximately $36 million. By November 2016 the parent entity had renamed itself CleanSpark, Inc., ticker CLSK, trading on OTC markets. The company listed on the Nasdaq Capital Market in January 2020.

Zach Bradford joined as CFO and President during the energy-software era. On **October 10, 2019**, Bradford was promoted to CEO and President, with co-founder Matthew Schultz moving to Executive Chairman. That leadership configuration would define the company's subsequent trajectory. The energy-software business — microgrid controls, distributed energy resource management — provided the operational DNA for what came next: a company that knew how to procure, manage, and monetize electricity at scale.

## The Bitcoin Mining Pivot, December 2020

The pivot arrived in a single transaction. On **December 10, 2020**, CleanSpark announced an agreement to acquire ATL Data Centers, LLC, a Bitcoin mining operation located in College Park, Georgia, near Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport, for up to **$19.4 million in common stock**. At closing, ATL operated 3,471 ASICs generating approximately 190 PH/s across roughly 9.6 MW of capacity. Power cost at the Georgia site was targeted below **$0.0285 per kilowatt-hour** — a figure that underscored the energy-first logic Bradford had carried over from the microgrid era.

Executive Chairman Schultz framed the ambition plainly at the time: *"This transaction should immediately position us as one of the largest publicly-traded Bitcoin producers in the country."* CleanSpark planned to expand the College Park campus from 20 MW to 50 MW, projecting a future hash rate of 0.9–1.4 EH/s from that single site.

## Scaling Through an ATM-Funded Land Grab, 2021–2023

CleanSpark funded its expansion principally through equity capital markets. In March 2021 the company completed an underwritten public offering of 9,090,910 shares at **$22.00 per share**, generating approximately **$200 million** in gross proceeds. Three months later it entered an at-the-market offering agreement with H.C. Wainwright & Co. — capacity up to $500 million in common stock — which it drew on continuously; by late 2022 it had raised **$219.7 million** under the program before amending and resetting capacity to $500 million again. The ATM structure gave Bradford a perpetual capital tool that kept dilution piecemeal but kept the balance sheet funded through every hardware acquisition cycle.

By **January 24, 2022**, CleanSpark announced it had crossed **2 EH/s** in operating hash rate, doubling in three months, with daily Bitcoin production of roughly 10 BTC. The Georgia footprint expanded from College Park into Norcross and Washington. Bradford noted: *"We have more capacity coming, in terms of both machines and access to additional energy."* Schultz captured the competitive logic with characteristic directness: *"Given how much network difficulty is increasing, if you're not growing, you're regressing."*

The next step-change came via acquisition. On **October 8, 2022**, CleanSpark closed the purchase of Mawson Infrastructure Group's Sandersville, Georgia facility for **$34.3 million** at closing (including approximately 1.59 million CLSK shares), plus an additional $9.48 million for 6,468 ASIC miners. The deal added roughly **560 PH/s** and pushed aggregate operating hash rate to **4.7 EH/s** across four Georgia campuses. Sandersville carried a long-term buildout potential of **230 MW / 7.0 EH/s** at full capacity. Bradford set a public target: *"We are looking forward to eventually building this site to its full potential of 230 MW as we work toward our 2023 year-end guidance of 22.4 EH/s."*

Fiscal year 2023 (ending September 30, 2023) produced **$168.4 million in revenue** — 28 percent year-over-year growth — with **6,903 BTC mined**, up 84 percent. CleanSpark crossed the **10 EH/s** threshold and posted adjusted EBITDA of **$25.0 million**, though the net loss remained deep at $(136.6) million, reflecting depreciation, impairment, and the cost of a fleet that was still burning through first-generation hardware.

## Pre-Halving Discipline and the S21 Generation, 2023–2024

CleanSpark entered 2024 knowing the Bitcoin halving — the scheduled reduction in per-block reward from 6.25 BTC to 3.125 BTC — would compress unit economics sector-wide. Bradford's stated thesis was unambiguous: the survivors would be the operators with the lowest electricity cost and the newest, most efficient fleets.

In **October 2023**, CleanSpark acquired **4.4 EH/s worth of new Bitmain Antminer S21 miners** for **$12.35 million** ($2.80 per terahash), with delivery scheduled for January 2024. The S21 ran at **17.5 J/TH** — approximately 20 percent more efficient than the prior-generation XP — and immediately became the fleet's efficiency anchor. Bradford described the rationale: *"The efficiency of the S21 should not only increase our capacity but also drive down energy costs per bitcoin mined, enhancing our competitive edge."*

By **April 12, 2024** — one week before the halving — CleanSpark had surpassed **17 EH/s** in operating hash rate and exercised an option to purchase **100,000 Bitmain Antminer S21 Pro miners**, representing an additional **23.4 EH/s** of purchased capacity. The S21 Pro improved efficiency to **15 J/TH**, a further 14 percent improvement over the base S21, at the same $16/TH unit price. Bradford declared: *"With the upgrade to the new S21 Pro, we expect that we have cemented our lead as the most efficient publicly traded bitcoin miner at scale in North America."*

The halving hit on **April 19–20, 2024**. CleanSpark entered it with 17 EH/s deployed, S21 Pros in the delivery pipeline through December, and a Georgia-anchored power portfolio priced well below the industry average.

## 30 EH/s, GRIID, and the XP Immersion Layer, 2024

The twelve months following the halving became CleanSpark's most aggressive buildout period on record. In **May 2024** the company acquired two Wyoming sites totaling 75 MW for $18.75 million, projecting more than 4 EH/s from the new footprint. In **June 2024**, five additional rural Georgia facilities changed hands for $25.8 million, adding 3.7 EH/s. In **August 2024**, CleanSpark purchased **26,000 Bitmain Antminer S21 XP immersion-cooled units** — 300 TH/s per unit, running at 13.5 J/TH — for a total of **$167.7 million** ($21.50/TH), adding approximately 7.8 EH/s to purchased capacity.

On **October 10, 2024**, CleanSpark announced it had crossed **30 EH/s** in operating hash rate, representing 200 percent growth since October 2023. Bradford stated: *"Reaching 30 EH/s positions us as one of the largest bitcoin miners in the world. We have added more operational hashrate than any other miner in 2024."* Twenty days later, on **October 30, 2024**, the company closed its acquisition of **GRIID Infrastructure** — seven Tennessee facilities totaling 85 MW and approximately 5 EH/s — following stockholder approval on October 28. Tennessee added geographic diversification beyond the Georgia core.

Fiscal year 2024 (ending September 30, 2024) delivered **$378.9 million in revenue**, up 125 percent year-over-year, with adjusted EBITDA reaching **$245.8 million** versus $25.0 million the prior year. The balance sheet held **8,049 BTC** valued at $509.5 million as of September 30, alongside 726 MW of operating power capacity — up 423 MW during the fiscal year. Total assets reached **$2.0 billion**.

In **December 2024**, CleanSpark simultaneously announced a **37.5 EH/s** operating milestone and priced a **$650 million zero-coupon convertible note** — proceeds earmarked to fully fund the path to 50 EH/s and build out remaining S21 XP capacity. Bradford summarized the year: *"We have delivered on our ambitious targets and expanded our hashrate nearly 300% since the beginning of 2024."*

## Forward Catalysts: 50 EH/s, AI/HPC Optionality, and Leadership Transition

By January 2025, CleanSpark held **10,556 BTC** in treasury, operated **217,272 miners**, and averaged **34.76 EH/s** — crossing **40 EH/s** at month-end. Fleet-wide efficiency stood at **17.37 J/TH** on average as S21 XP immersion units progressively replaced earlier-generation hardware.

In **August 2025**, Bradford stepped down as CEO — receiving a $950,000 separation payment, 14.4 BTC, and a prorated 2025 bonus of approximately $1.58 million — with Schultz returning to the CEO role he had originally held from 2014 to 2019. The transition completed a full circle: the co-founder who had seeded the energy-software pivot returning to lead the company Bradford had built into a multi-EH/s mining operator.

| Milestone | Date | Hash Rate | Key Detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| ATL Data Centers acquisition | Dec 2020 | 190 PH/s | First Bitcoin mining entry, College Park GA |
| 2 EH/s | Jan 2022 | 2 EH/s | ~10 BTC/day; Norcross campus active |
| Sandersville (Mawson) close | Oct 2022 | 4.7 EH/s | 4th Georgia campus; $34.3M |
| 10 EH/s | FY2023 | 10 EH/s | $168.4M revenue; first S21 purchase |
| 17 EH/s + S21 Pro order | Apr 2024 | 17 EH/s | Pre-halving; 100K S21 Pros at 15 J/TH |
| 30 EH/s | Oct 2024 | 30 EH/s | +200% YoY; GRIID Tennessee close |
| 37.5 EH/s | Dec 2024 | 37.5 EH/s | $650M zero-coupon convert |
| 40+ EH/s | Jan 2025 | 40.1 EH/s | 10,556 BTC treasury |

The AI/HPC pivot, long characterized as "optionality" under Bradford, sharpened into formal strategy under Schultz. In **October 2025**, CleanSpark announced the acquisition of approximately **271 acres in Austin County, Texas** — between Houston and Austin — carrying **285 MW of long-term power agreements** earmarked for AI data center development. With substation construction underway and **200-plus MW energization targeted for H1 2027**, the Texas campus represented a 28 percent increase in total power under contract. Advanced conversations for AI/HPC hosting at Sandersville, Georgia — a 250 MW campus — were simultaneously reported in analyst coverage, with an investment-grade hyperscaler cited as the prospective counterparty. The power-secured campus footprint that Bradford had spent five years assembling, principally as a Bitcoin mining asset base, had become the underlying commodity for a second act Bradford himself would not lead.

chapters.title: Energy procurement know-how, fleet management software, data center operations IP
chapters.body:
## From Microgrid Software to Mining NOC

CleanSpark's operational edge in 2024–2025 was not accidental engineering — it was the accumulated residue of an earlier corporate life. Before Zach Bradford pivoted the company decisively toward Bitcoin mining, CleanSpark spent the better part of a decade building, patenting, and selling grid-intelligence software. That heritage left an institutional reflex for thinking about electricity as a dynamic variable to be optimized rather than a fixed utility bill to be paid.

The flagship product of that era was **mPulse**, a software-and-controls package that collected, archived, and analysed real-time data across distributed energy resources and microgrid installations. Alongside it ran **Fractalgrid** — a patented architecture (U.S. Patent 9,941,696 B2, issued April 2018) that spread decision-making intelligence through a hybrid cloud/semi-autonomous grid topology, enabling peak shaving, load shifting, and machine-learning responses to weather and demand changes. The company ranked in Navigant's top-ten microgrid-controls leaderboard, ahead of GE, ABB, Eaton, and Lockheed Martin. A second patent (U.S. Patent 10,658,839, issued May 2020) covered the logic by which a networked module forecasts its own future power needs to decide "if and when to share power with another module" — a control-intelligence claim that management later said [remained relevant](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/investing/markets/stocks/CLSK/pressreleases/1861154/cleanspark-clsk-q2-2026-earnings-transcript/) to its Bitcoin mining infrastructure: *"The patent basically says that the control module has the ability to make a decision if and when to distribute power to a requesting module."*

In Q3 2022 CleanSpark classified the energy software division as discontinued operations, wrote down $10.6 million in goodwill, and sold or disposed of mPulse, mVoult, and the OpenADR platform GridFabric. The balance-sheet IP walked out the door. What stayed was harder to sell: the engineers, the procurement instincts, and the habit of treating power as a negotiable input.

## Fleet Management: The Henderson NOC

The operational nervous system of CleanSpark's mining estate by late 2025 was a [control and analytics centre](https://investors.cleanspark.com/news/news-details/2024/CleanSpark-Names-Chief-Operating-Officer-and-Chief-Technology-Officer/default.aspx) at Henderson, Nevada headquarters, described as "home to the core technology team" that remotely monitors the company's 30-plus sites. The facility functioned as a network-operations centre for 245,199 deployed miners across Georgia, Mississippi, Tennessee, New York, and Wyoming.

Leading that centre was Chief Operating Officer Taylor Monnig, who before CleanSpark had co-founded TMGCore and served as its COO, developing the **OTTO** two-phase immersion-cooling platform — a system that won Intel's 2020 Datacenter Solutions Group Partner Award and packed 11,500 CPU cores and 120 kW of compute into under 70 square feet, claiming 80% cooling-energy reduction versus conventional air-cooled architecture. Monnig holds data-centre patents from that period. On the hardware engineering side, VP Technology Tyler Kostun brought a background in Applied Physics from Georgia Tech, high-voltage power equipment experience at Hitachi T&D Solutions, and high-energy particle physics research. He joined CleanSpark as one of its first on-site technicians and built the technology organisation from first principles.

The fleet management logic running out of Henderson was dynamic and multi-variable. Per the [Q1 FY2026 earnings call](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/02/05/cleanspark-clsk-q1-2026-earnings-call-transcript/), management disclosed that the technology team ran "real-time analysis based on utility prices, network difficulty and the price of Bitcoin," toggling three operational modes across the fleet: underclocking by an average of 27% to reduce consumption when economics tightened, maintaining standard operation, or overclocking to add roughly 12% incremental hashrate at no additional energy consumption. At a Bitcoin price near $63,000, less than 10% of the fleet was operating below breakeven — a testament to how closely the optimisation logic tracked unit profitability in real time. Across wholly-owned sites, the company reported [99.87% uptime](https://s203.q4cdn.com/737227956/files/doc_presentations/2024/Aug/30/fy2024-q3-investor-presentation-august.pdf) as of FY2023, a benchmark that underpinned the fleet efficiency figures: an average of 16.07 joules per terahash by December 2025, down from 26.4 J/Th in FY2023.

## Energy Procurement: The Interruptible-Load Thesis

CleanSpark's energy procurement strategy rested on a deliberately cultivated value proposition to utilities: industrial-scale flexible load that could be curtailed at short notice, absorbing excess generation and releasing capacity during demand spikes. Co-founder and CEO Matt Schultz articulated the logic in the [Q3 FY2025 earnings call](https://www.investing.com/news/transcripts/earnings-call-transcript-cleanspark-q3-2025-beats-eps-forecast-stock-rises-93CH-4179941):

> "Adding just 100 hours per year of flexibility to the grid could solve the vast majority of rolling brownouts and rolling blackouts that utilities face. We approach a utility with a flexible load in mind. And the flexibility is an asset in their portfolio."

In practice that translated to interruptible-load-designated power purchase agreements across multiple states. Georgia, the principal operating footprint with roughly 620 MW of active capacity by late 2025, provided some of the most favourable terms: all-in power costs of $0.043–$0.048 per kWh in FY2024, with wholesale rates at some wholly-owned sites reaching as low as $0.013 per kWh (1.3 cents), as President and CFO Gary Vecchiarelli disclosed in the [Q2 FY2024 call](https://s203.q4cdn.com/737227956/files/doc_presentations/2024/Aug/30/fy2024-q3-investor-presentation-august.pdf). The access to Plant Vogtle's nuclear output was a structural feature: *"Access to Nuclear Energy is one of the principal reasons we've made Georgia our home."*

A structural procurement advantage in Georgia derived partly from personnel. VP of Construction and Engineering Brian Jaynes spent fifteen years as VP of Engineering at Electric Cities of Georgia (ECG), the technical assistance body for Georgia's public-power utilities. [ECG and CleanSpark collaborated directly](https://ecoga.org/2022/11/02/cleanspark-hosts-media-and-dignitary-day-at-bitcoin-mining-facility-in-norcross/) to develop optimal power solutions for each community, with ECG providing data analytics, cost-risk modelling, and engineering support — an institutional relationship that compressed the negotiation cycle that outside operators would face cold.

The procurement structure itself evolved. By the [Q2 FY2026 call](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/investing/markets/stocks/CLSK/pressreleases/1861154/cleanspark-clsk-q2-2026-earnings-transcript/), Chief Business Officer Harry Sudock described a utility-intermediated model where the electric membership cooperative acted as the market-facing procurement agent for CleanSpark's contracted load: *"The utility goes out to market and procures the power over duration, directly for the contracted demand that we represent. By moving into that procurement method, they mitigate the community risk for any pass back because they are procuring that power on the open market."* The arrangement hedged both parties against spot-price volatility.

The TVA relationship in Tennessee — expanded materially through the October 2024 [GRIID Infrastructure acquisition](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/cleanspark-announces-agreement-to-acquire-griid-infrastructure-based-on-an-enterprise-value-of-155-million-and-expansion-plans-of-over-400-mw-in-tennessee-302184116.html) at $155 million enterprise value — demonstrated the demand-response capability in live conditions. In December 2025, during extreme cold weather across the TVA service territory, the technology team powered down eleven Tennessee sites within ten minutes of TVA's curtailment request, using a [customised communications integration](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/cleanspark-releases-december-2025-bitcoin-mining-update-302653478.html) built specifically for TVA's dispatch protocols. Chief Development Officer Scott Garrison called it: *"Our ability to respond rapidly reflects the depth of our technology, expertise, and operational discipline."*

## Data Centre Operations and the Pivot Infrastructure

On the physical infrastructure side, CleanSpark ran a dual-track operation: conventional air-cooled facilities at most Georgia, Mississippi, and Tennessee sites, and an expanding immersion-cooled tier anchored by the 20-MW Norcross, Georgia facility — 87,000 square feet, 180 liquid-filled tanks, cooled with a biodegradable synthetic hydrocarbon that the company claimed reduced e-waste by 85% versus air-cooled equivalents. A second fully immersion-cooled campus followed in [Cheyenne, Wyoming](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/cleanspark-executes-75-mw-of-power-contracts-and-completes-acquisition-of-bitcoin-mining-site-in-wyoming-302212200.html), deploying Bitmain S21 XP Immersion units at 13.5 J/Th. By Q1 FY2026, modular immersion-cooled containers were being simultaneously deployed across five locations.

For the AI/HPC pivot, CleanSpark developed what management described as a factory-build model for data centre MEP (mechanical, electrical, and plumbing) packages: "60% to 70% of the data centre build we are contemplating takes place in a factory," with the gray shell constructed on-site to chipset-manufacturer specifications and the MEP package prefabricated off-site for consistency. The architecture had received reference approval from chipset manufacturers, enabling chip-type flexibility without facility redesign. The 14-to-18-month delivery window from lease signing compared to three to six years for traditional data-centre construction — a speed advantage that Schultz credited directly when CleanSpark won a [Wyoming 100 MW AI contract over Microsoft](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/10/28/bitcoin-miner-cleanspark-crypto-mining-energy-power-ai-data-center.html).

The Submer [strategic partnership announced in 2025](https://investors.cleanspark.com/news/news-details/2025/CleanSpark-Selects-Submer-as-Its-First-Strategic-Partner-for-AI-Data-Center-Expansion-in-North-America/default.aspx) layered in third-party liquid-cooling systems, power modules, and facility construction capability on top of CleanSpark's own power-secured land portfolio. Schultz described the combination as positioning the company to "deliver AI capacity at gigawatt scale, faster, cleaner, and more efficiently than traditional approaches." Taken together — the energy-software intellectual ancestry, the Henderson NOC's real-time optimisation stack, the decade of interruptible-load PPA structuring, and the emerging factory-build data-centre model — CleanSpark's operational IP resided less in registered patent claims than in a set of engineering instincts and utility relationships that proved difficult to replicate at speed.

chapters.title: Bitcoin price cycle, halving impact, electricity cost, AI/HPC execution, competitive, scale
chapters.body:
## Bitcoin Price Cycle: The Unavoidable Coefficient

CleanSpark's entire operating model reduces, in the final analysis, to a single multiplication: hash rate deployed, times the fraction of network reward captured, times the spot price of Bitcoin at the moment of sale. That last variable — Bitcoin price — is one the company can neither hedge, control, nor substantially offset through operational discipline alone. The consequence is a revenue line that behaves like a leveraged derivative on an asset that has historically oscillated between drawdowns exceeding eighty percent and multi-year parabolic recoveries.

The 2022 crypto winter illustrated the severity. Bitcoin's collapse from roughly $69,000 in November 2021 to below $16,000 in late 2022 triggered a wave of miner bankruptcies and fire-sale ASIC liquidations across the industry. CleanSpark navigated that cycle without a balance-sheet collapse — a function of its comparatively low electricity cost base and continued access to equity capital markets — but the experience reinforced what the company's own SEC filings acknowledge explicitly: revenue and profitability are materially dependent on the price of Bitcoin, over which management has no influence. In a protracted bear market, even a well-run operator with sub-3 cents per kilowatt-hour power and a fully refreshed S21-generation fleet will generate operating losses if Bitcoin trades at levels that render the per-coin mining cost above the market price. The equity, carrying no contractual cash-flow protections, absorbs that volatility in full.

## Halving Economics: The Structural Compression That Doesn't Reverse

The April 2024 halving — the fourth in Bitcoin's protocol history — cut the per-block subsidy from 6.25 BTC to 3.125 BTC overnight. For an operator running a fixed power cost and a fixed infrastructure base, the effect was arithmetically simple and operationally brutal: every joule of electricity consumed now produced half the Bitcoin reward it had twelve hours earlier. The industry response was consolidation, fleet refresh, and a renewed focus on operational efficiency metrics that had been somewhat overlooked during the 2023 recovery.

CleanSpark responded with an accelerated push into the Bitmain Antminer S21 and S21 XP generation — ASICs that deliver materially lower joules-per-terahash figures than the prior S19 cohort — and with a stated commitment to post-halving operating discipline. The efficiency improvement is real, but it addresses only the joules side of the unit-economics equation; it cannot restore the block subsidy itself. The deeper structural risk is that each successive halving, arriving approximately every four years, compresses the subsidy further while transaction fees — the long-run replacement revenue stream in Bitcoin's protocol design — remain insufficient to fully compensate at current network utilization levels. CleanSpark's long-run viability as a pure-play miner depends on Bitcoin's price appreciation outpacing this structural subsidy decay, a thesis with historical support but no guarantee.

## Electricity Cost: The Competitive Moat With Counterparty Risk

Low-cost electricity is CleanSpark's most defensible competitive asset. The company has built its Georgia-centric operating footprint around long-term power purchase agreements and direct utility arrangements that, at their best, deliver all-in power costs below $0.04 per kilowatt-hour — a figure that places it among the lowest-cost operators in the public peer set. At those rates, the post-halving unit economics remain positive across a meaningful range of Bitcoin prices.

The risk is that this moat is neither permanent nor frictionless. Power purchase agreements expire. Utilities renegotiate. Regulators in Georgia, Mississippi, Tennessee, and other operating states can revise rate structures, impose demand charges, or restrict commercial mining load. More immediately, the AI/HPC infrastructure buildout — which CleanSpark itself hopes to benefit from as a potential pivot — is simultaneously driving up demand for the same low-cost, large-block power that the company depends on, tightening supply and increasing the cost of new capacity additions. A competitor with deeper pockets or a more attractive grid-impact profile could outbid CleanSpark for the next tranche of PPA capacity. Any material increase in the all-in electricity cost — whether from PPA expiry, regulatory action, or competitive power market tightening — flows directly to operating margin with no natural offset.

## AI/HPC Execution: Optionality Without a Proven Track Record

CleanSpark's management has identified the company's power-secured campus footprint as a potential foundation for AI/HPC hosting, a pivot thesis that several peers — Core Scientific (CORZ), Iris Energy (IREN), and TeraWulf (WULF) in particular — have pursued with varying degrees of urgency and disclosed customer engagement. The optionality is genuine: colocation-ready infrastructure with secured power interconnects is genuinely scarce and genuinely sought by hyperscalers and AI-focused compute operators.

The execution risk, however, is substantial. CleanSpark's track record is in Bitcoin mining, not in enterprise data center operations, colocation contracting, or high-density cooling infrastructure — the physical and operational requirements of AI/HPC hosting are meaningfully different from ASIC-based mining. Signing a hyperscaler or an AI pure-play to a multi-year hosting contract requires both infrastructure credibility and sales relationships that the company is still developing. Core Scientific's head start — including its disclosed agreements with CoreWeave — illustrates the gap between announcing optionality and realizing contracted revenue. Every quarter CleanSpark spends allocating its capital primarily to hash rate expansion rather than AI/HPC infrastructure build-out is a quarter in which the competitive window for the most attractive hosting contracts potentially narrows.

## Competitive Positioning: A Crowded Field Scaling Simultaneously

The public Bitcoin mining peer set is scaling simultaneously, and the race to multi-EH/s target rates is being run by multiple well-capitalized operators at once.

| Peer | Primary Strategy | AI/HPC Disclosed |
|---|---|---|
| Riot Platforms (RIOT) | Hash rate scale; Corsicana Texas campus | Limited |
| Marathon Digital (MARA) | Hash rate scale; BTC treasury strategy | Limited |
| Core Scientific (CORZ) | AI/HPC pivot; CoreWeave contracts | Active |
| Iris Energy (IREN) | AI/HPC hosting; GPU cloud | Active |
| TeraWulf (WULF) | Nuclear-powered campus; AI optionality | Developing |
| Bitfarms (BITF) | International diversification | Limited |

In this context, CleanSpark's competitive differentiation rests primarily on electricity cost discipline and operational uptime — genuine advantages, but ones that are replicated in varying degrees by Riot's Corsicana buildout and by IREN's Australian and North American campus network. Network difficulty — which adjusts upward as the aggregate industry hash rate grows — erodes the hash-rate advantage of every new exahash added to the network, requiring constant re-investment simply to maintain market share of the block reward. The treadmill dynamic means CleanSpark must continue deploying capital into ASIC procurement and power infrastructure at pace with or ahead of the network, or see its share of the reward pool shrink.

## Scale Execution: Capital Access, Dilution, and the ATM Dependency

Hash rate scaling at the pace CleanSpark has pursued requires continuous capital deployment — into ASICs, into power infrastructure, into data center civil works. The company has funded this buildout principally through at-the-market equity issuance facilities, a mechanism that provides flexible access to capital markets but generates ongoing shareholder dilution. In a rising Bitcoin price environment, dilution is offset by share price appreciation; in a bear market, the same equity issuance occurs at depressed prices, compounding value destruction.

The ATM-dependency also creates a sensitivity to equity market sentiment that operating miners without alternative capital sources cannot easily escape. A prolonged period of depressed Bitcoin prices, combined with broader risk-off conditions in equity markets, could simultaneously reduce the cash flow available from mining operations and impair CleanSpark's ability to access equity capital on acceptable terms — a scenario in which planned capex programs would face curtailment. The company carries no substantial long-term fixed-rate debt structure that might otherwise insulate it from equity market volatility. Scaling ambitions and capital structure resilience exist in tension: the faster management pushes hash rate growth, the more dependent the execution becomes on continued equity market access at prices that justify the dilution.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## The calendar ahead

CleanSpark's fiscal year closes each September 30, setting a drumbeat of four quarterly filings between the frozen snapshot and the end of fiscal 2027. The FY2026 third-quarter result — covering April through June 2026 — was expected to reach the market around early August 2026; the FY2026 annual result in late November; and FY2027 first and second quarters in February and May 2027, respectively. Sitting above the formal filings, the company's monthly operational updates, published within the first weeks of each following month, disclosed BTC produced, hash rate installed, and fleet statistics — creating twelve additional near-term catalysts that often moved the stock more abruptly than the quarterly reports themselves.

The most consequential pending milestone as of the frozen snapshot was not a quarterly print but a strategic pivot decision: the timing and scope of CleanSpark's first material AI/HPC hosting commitment. By May 2026, Core Scientific, TeraWulf, and Iris Energy had each contracted significant high-performance computing hosting capacity, rerating their equity toward data-center multiples for the committed portion of their footprint. CleanSpark had maintained an evaluative posture, publicly framing its power-secured Georgia and Wyoming campuses as optionality rather than committed capacity — a disciplined stance that preserved Bitcoin mining yield but left the AI/HPC upside unpriced in the equity. An announcement crystallizing even one or two hundred megawatts of HPC hosting would represent the single largest binary catalyst in the forward twelve months, independent of Bitcoin price.

## Hash rate and fleet efficiency milestones

From its multi-EH/s operating base at the frozen snapshot, CleanSpark was targeting continued scaling through deployments of the Bitmain Antminer S21 Pro and S21 XP generations — the efficiency frontier at approximately 15–17 joules per terahash — which, at scale, implied a materially lower operating cost per BTC mined relative to the S19-era fleet being retired. The watch-items on this axis were threefold: monthly BTC produced per installed exahash (fleet utilization and uptime), fleet-average efficiency in joules per terahash (the pace of S19 retirement and S21 XP deployment), and site-level curtailment events from grid conditions or equipment downtime.

Each monthly operational update served as a real-time checkpoint before the quarterly P&L arrived. A month in which BTC produced per installed EH/s declined without a maintenance, upgrade, or grid-curtailment explanation was a leading indicator of fleet-economics deterioration, typically visible six to ten weeks before the quarterly filing confirmed it in accounting terms.

| Metric | Bear Case | Base Case | Bull Case |
|---|---|---|---|
| Exit EH/s (end FY2027) | 45–50 | 55–65 | 70–80 |
| Fleet-avg. efficiency (J/TH) | 18–21 | 15–18 | 13–15 |
| All-in electricity cost ($/MWh) | $40–48 | $30–40 | $25–32 |
| All-in cost per BTC mined | $45,000–65,000 | $30,000–45,000 | $20,000–30,000 |

The all-in cost per BTC mined is the single most load-bearing number in the operating model. It sets the Bitcoin price floor below which gross profit turns negative, determines the pace of ATM equity issuance required to fund operations and capex, and defines the competitive moat versus operators whose older fleets and higher electricity costs push their breakeven hundreds of dollars per coin higher.

## Consensus estimates and the operating-economics lens

CleanSpark does not publish formal revenue guidance, and Wall Street consensus on Bitcoin mining operators carries unusually wide dispersion because the principal revenue variable — Bitcoin price — is itself unforecastable. Sell-side estimates for FY2026 (ending September 30, 2026) ranged from approximately $600 million on the low end to above $1.0 billion under constructive Bitcoin price scenarios, with implied full-year growth rates depending almost entirely on where BTC settled relative to the prior-year average. FY2027 estimates extended the range further, with the AI/HPC optionality creating a potential revenue layer above the pure-mining base case that sell-side central scenarios had not yet fully incorporated at the snapshot date.

The more actionable consensus metric was the implied gross profit per BTC mined under the base-case cost structure. At a Bitcoin network difficulty level implying breakeven for S19-generation operators in the mid-to-high $50,000s per coin, an S21 XP fleet with sub-$35/MWh electricity would theoretically sustain a gross margin cushion of $35,000–$55,000 per BTC at Bitcoin prices in the $90,000–$110,000 range. The confirmation or denial of that margin band in the quarterly cost disclosures was the central beat-or-miss signal each reporting cycle.

## What beats and misses look like

A beat against prevailing expectations required three simultaneous signals to arrive together: BTC produced per month at or above the level implied by disclosed installed hash rate, confirming high fleet utilization and minimal curtailment; all-in electricity cost at or below the $30–35/MWh band publicly associated with the company's Georgia PPA portfolio; and either a first AI/HPC hosting announcement or concrete management language in the earnings call indicating a customer agreement was near completion.

A miss manifested through any one of three failure modes. BTC produced declining quarter-over-quarter without a maintenance or site-upgrade explanation signaled curtailment degradation or fleet downtime before the income statement captured it. Electricity cost per MWh creeping above $40, whether through spot-market exposure at newly acquired sites or regulatory cost pressures in one of the operating jurisdictions, compressed the margin cushion that justified the premium multiple versus lower-quality peers. And a quarterly ATM share issuance materially larger than capex requirements justified — signaling balance-sheet stress camouflaged in the headline GAAP line — was perhaps the most insidious form of miss, one that did not announce itself loudly but accumulated in per-share dilution.

The most asymmetric potential negative was a network difficulty spike outpacing fleet efficiency improvement. If the broader industrial mining fleet installed hash rate faster than CleanSpark completed its S21 XP rollout — a pattern that materialized intermittently across 2024 and 2025 as North American and international operators added capacity in waves — the per-BTC cost advantage would narrow and the operational thesis would revert from best-in-class efficiency narrative toward commodity mining, commanding a lower multiple.

## The bull and bear setup

The bull case rested on three pillars at the frozen snapshot. The company's structural cost position — energy procurement discipline through long-term PPAs, fleet efficiency improvement through the S21 XP generation, and geographic site diversity across Georgia, Mississippi, Wyoming, and Tennessee — placed it among the sector's demonstrable low-cost operators, creating resilience through Bitcoin price volatility that peer-average operators could not replicate without access to equivalent power purchase terms. The AI/HPC pivot optionality embedded in that power-secured campus footprint represented unpriced upside: if a hosting agreement crystallized at the data-center economics peers such as Core Scientific were already realizing — long-term contracted revenue at $200–$350 per megawatt-hour compared with the $50–$80 effective revenue equivalent from Bitcoin mining at prevailing prices — the rerate of even modest committed capacity would add material present-value uplift to the equity story without requiring Bitcoin to cooperate. And Bitcoin's four-year halving cycle, if it followed historical patterns of sustained price appreciation in the eighteen-to-thirty months following a halving event, provided a macro tailwind that pure-play operators with the lowest cost floors were structurally best positioned to harvest in operating cash flow terms.

The bear case was structural rather than merely cyclical. Peer operators — Core Scientific most prominently, but also TeraWulf and Iris Energy — had committed earlier and more aggressively to AI/HPC hosting, potentially locking in tier-1 hyperscaler demand before CleanSpark reached a decision; a late-mover disadvantage in securing long-duration HPC contracts would leave the company fully exposed to Bitcoin price beta, with less diversification credit than its rerating peers commanded at their new multiples. The bear also noted that ATM equity issuance, while kept off the income statement as a cash item, had compounded share count meaningfully over the prior three years; in a scenario where Bitcoin price compressed and operating cash flow deteriorated, the issuance rate would accelerate and per-share intrinsic value improvement would stall or reverse regardless of operational execution quality.

The asymmetry at the frozen snapshot tilted modestly toward the bull scenario on a twelve-month horizon. The company held enough structural cost advantage to survive a moderate Bitcoin price drawdown without triggering balance-sheet distress. The AI/HPC optionality was unpriced rather than negatively valued — a feature embedded in the power footprint, not a liability, even if the crystallization timeline remained uncertain through mid-2026. Zach Bradford's track record of executing the hash rate scaling plan — from a handful of EH/s in 2022 through to a scaled multi-EH/s operation by 2025–2026 — without catastrophic equity dilution or debt accumulation provided management credibility that constrained the severity of the downside scenario. The highest-conviction upside path to a material equity re-rating through calendar 2027 ran through an AI/HPC announcement layered onto continued Bitcoin price stability — a combination that remained the central probability-weighted scenario rather than an optimistic outlier at the snapshot date.

chapters.title: Hash rate scaling, AI/HPC pivot, fleet refresh, 2026-2030 horizon

## The scaling trajectory and the halving test

CleanSpark's multi-year hash rate expansion reached a strategic inflection in April 2024 when the fourth Bitcoin halving compressed the per-block protocol reward from 6.25 bitcoin to 3.125 bitcoin — halving the gross revenue per unit of computational work deployed across the network. For operators that had not refreshed their fleets ahead of the event, the economics were punishing. CleanSpark had spent the preceding eighteen months accelerating deployment of Bitmain Antminer S21-generation hardware — the S21, S21 Pro, and S21 XP — which delivered materially lower joule-per-terahash ratios than the S19 generation they replaced. The result was that CleanSpark entered the halving with a fleet efficiency profile that allowed it to sustain positive mining margins even as the reward subsidy halved.

The strategic significance of that preparation extended beyond the immediate earnings quarter. By demonstrating operating discipline at the inflection point, CleanSpark signalled to capital markets that its management team — led since 2017 by chief executive Zach Bradford, who guided the company through its full evolution from energy-software operator to pure-play Bitcoin miner — could manage the cyclical stress inherent in the business model. The company's funding architecture, principally through at-the-money equity issuance via successive ATM shelf facilities filed with the SEC, gave it access to capital even during price drawdowns, provided the equity market held confidence in management's execution track record.

## Fleet refresh: the perpetual efficiency race

The economics of industrial Bitcoin mining are governed by a relentless logic: every generation of ASIC hardware is eventually superseded by a more efficient successor, and operators who delay fleet refresh find their cost curves drifting above network difficulty-adjusted breakevens. CleanSpark's capital allocation through 2024-2025 reflected that logic directly. The shift toward the S21 XP — Bitmain's highest-efficiency hardware available through the snapshot window — represented the latest iteration of what had become a systematic refresh discipline.

The fleet refresh cycle creates a recurring capital commitment that must be funded through the combination of operating cash flow and equity issuance. During favourable Bitcoin price environments, CleanSpark generated operating cash flows sufficient to partially self-fund expansion. During drawdown periods, the ATM facility became the marginal funding mechanism. Management's stated preference, articulated across multiple earnings calls, was to use equity issuance as a bridge rather than a structural dependence — a posture that required demonstrating hash rate growth against which the dilution could be measured and justified to institutional shareholders.

The next-generation hardware cycle beyond S21 XP — whether from Bitmain, MicroBT Whatsminer, or emerging ASIC manufacturers — will define CleanSpark's fleet refresh capex cadence through 2026-2028. The company's procurement relationships with Bitmain, built through successive large purchase orders during the 2022-2025 scaling cycle, represent a channel advantage that smaller operators cannot easily replicate. Whether those relationships translate into preferential allocation of next-generation hardware at launch — a historically significant competitive variable in an industry where early deployment of a more efficient generation can create durable cost advantages before rivals catch up — remained a watching brief as of the snapshot window.

## The power moat and campus footprint

CleanSpark's competitive differentiation rested substantially on the quality and structure of its energy procurement. The company's Georgia footprint — established through a series of site acquisitions and greenfield builds across the state — was structured around long-term power purchase agreements with utilities and independent power producers that locked in all-in electricity costs at rates that management consistently described as among the most competitive in the US peer group. Electricity cost, measured in dollars per megawatt-hour, is the single most important operating variable for a Bitcoin miner: it sets the floor below which Bitcoin prices cannot fall without forcing curtailment or loss-generating operation.

The diversification beyond Georgia — into Mississippi, Tennessee, Wyoming, and New York — served multiple purposes simultaneously. It reduced single-state regulatory concentration risk, provided access to different power markets with varying seasonal and structural cost dynamics, and created a geographically distributed campus footprint that would prove strategically relevant if the AI/HPC optionality thesis were ever to be pursued in earnest. Each site represented a power-secured campus with high-voltage infrastructure, industrial cooling, and data centre buildout — assets financed primarily for Bitcoin mining but carrying latent value for alternative compute workloads should the economics warrant redeployment.

## The AI/HPC optionality question

Across the peer group, the AI/HPC pivot had become the defining strategic narrative of 2024-2025. Core Scientific signed a landmark hosting agreement with CoreWeave; Iris Energy pivoted toward GPU hosting with explicit AI/HPC branding and renamed its investor positioning accordingly; TeraWulf built out the Lake Mariner facility in upstate New York with AI/HPC capacity embedded in the development plan. The thesis was structurally coherent: power-secured campuses with existing high-voltage infrastructure, cooling systems, and fibre connectivity were scarce assets in an environment where hyperscalers and AI compute operators faced multi-year grid interconnection queues for new builds, and where the contracted power costs of an established Bitcoin miner could undercut greenfield data centre development economics substantially.

CleanSpark's posture on the question was more deliberate than many peers. Bradford and management had, through the 2024-2025 communications cycle, acknowledged the optionality without committing to a pivot timeline or capital allocation programme equivalent to Core Scientific or Iris Energy. The reasoning articulated was that CleanSpark's comparative advantage — vertically integrated Bitcoin mining at competitive unit economics — was most durable if pursued with focus, and that the AI/HPC opportunity, while structurally real, would require significant additional capital, a different customer development capability, and potential dilution of the pure-play Bitcoin mining identity that had been a deliberate investor positioning choice since the corporate pivot completed years earlier.

The optionality nevertheless remained embedded in the asset base. A power-secured campus at scale, with existing high-voltage interconnections and operational data centre infrastructure, does not require a formal AI/HPC strategy to carry latent conversion value. The question for 2026-2030 was whether the AI/HPC infrastructure buildout cycle — concentrated on the most aggressive forecasts through 2024-2027 — would move quickly enough, and at power economics demanding enough, to make conversion of Bitcoin mining capacity to AI/HPC hosting economically superior to continued mining expansion. That calculation depended on AI GPU hosting revenue rates, power costs, conversion capex, and the Bitcoin price trajectory simultaneously — a multi-variable optimisation that management showed no sign of resolving prematurely.

## The 2026-2030 strategic frame

The forward strategic posture visible as of the snapshot window described a company committed to three parallel disciplines. First, hash rate scaling: management's long-stated intention was to grow the company's share of the Bitcoin network hash rate, using fleet efficiency as the operational lever and long-term energy procurement as the cost moat. Second, capital discipline: the ATM-funded equity model required continuous demonstration that each incremental dollar of dilution was matched by incremental hash rate and — during favourable Bitcoin price environments — incremental operating cash flow. Third, optionality preservation: the company maintained the AI/HPC thesis as a strategic contingency without committing the capital reallocation that a full pivot would require.

| Strategic variable | CleanSpark posture (snapshot) | Key peers for comparison |
|---|---|---|
| Bitcoin mining focus | Pure-play maintained | MARA, RIOT (pure-play) |
| AI/HPC pivot commitment | Optionality acknowledged; no committed programme | CORZ, IREN (committed pivot); WULF (hybrid build) |
| Fleet generation | S21 XP deployed; next-gen pending | Peer-wide race to latest ASIC generation |
| Energy procurement | Long-term PPAs; Georgia principal footprint | RIOT Texas; IREN Australia/Texas |
| Capital structure | ATM equity + operating cash flow | Peer-wide ATM dependence post-halving |

The halving cycle places a structural clock on the strategic frame. The fifth halving — anticipated in approximately 2028 on Bitcoin's protocol-governed reward schedule — will compress the per-block reward from 3.125 BTC to 1.5625 BTC. At that point, only the lowest-cost operators with the highest-efficiency fleets will generate positive margins at prevailing network difficulty. CleanSpark's 2026-2030 positioning was explicitly oriented around that reality: scale hash rate before difficulty growth absorbs the advantage; refresh the fleet before the efficiency curve moves; lock in power at rates that survive another halving compression; and preserve the AI/HPC option as insurance against a scenario in which Bitcoin prices fail to recover sufficiently above the 2028 halving breakeven to sustain the pure-play model indefinitely.

Bradford had framed the competitive philosophy with consistent clarity across earnings communications: the Bitcoin mining industry rewards scale, efficiency, and patience in approximately that order. CleanSpark's investment in all three, funded through a capital markets strategy that had grown the company from a small-cap curiosity to a scaled NASDAQ-listed operator through successive halving cycles, would be tested against the 2028 event horizon with the same operating discipline that defined its navigation of April 2024.
